Resource sheet – Symbols of Federation
A national flag competition
In January 1911, Prime Minister Edmund Barton held a competition to design a flag to represent 
the new Commonwealth of Australia. Five joint winners shared the prize, and the flag was flown 
for the first time on 3 September 1901 at the Exhibition Building in Melbourne. 
A National Flag
The national flag question is becoming a warm one … opinions 
rage through the press as to what the flag should contain to make it 
emblematic. 
Someone wants bars, out of compliments to the States, which shouldn’t 
be entertained … Someone wants a kangaroo, but though this is typical 
enough, it is hoped that the successful artist will not embrace it, as the 
’roo looks ratty … One thing that should go on the flag is the Southern 
cross, with six stars, and each star would stand for a State without further 
embellishment. The “Jack” in the corner would complete a true heraldic 
design — the flag of a nation in the Pacific, affiliated with one in the 
North Sea. For official purposes the field could be blue, not too light and 
not too dark …
Source: Clarence and Richmond Examiner (Grafton, NSW: 1889–1915) Sat 27 Apr 1901, Page 4
Source 2 (About the design that won the competition)
… a staled réchauffé of the British flag, with no artistic virtue, no 
national significance ... Minds move slowly: and Australia is still Britain’s 
little boy. What more natural than that he should accept his father’s  
cut-down garments, — lacking the power to protest, and only dimly 
realising his will. That bastard flag is a true symbol of the bastard state of 
Australian opinion.
Source: The Bulletin magazine, 28 September 1901
Source 1 (Before the competition winners were announced)
Definition
réchauffé: a dish of warmed-up food, left over from a previous meal

We’re all Australians Now
In 1915, Andrew Barton ‘Banjo’ Paterson wrote the fourteen verse poem, ‘We’re all Australians Now’, 
as an open letter to Australian troops. 
In this poem, ‘Sydney’ is the battleship HMAS Sydney. This ship was flying the Australian flag when 
it defeated the German warship SMS Emden. 
Here are Verses 6, 7 and 14. 
Our six-starred flag that used 
to fly
Half shyly to the breeze,
Unknown where older 
nations ply
Their trade on foreign seas.
Flies out to meet the 
morning blue
With Victory at the prow;
For that’s the flag the Sydney 
flew,
The wide seas know it now!
And with Australia’s flag 
shall fly
A spray of wattle bough,
To symbolise our unity,
We’re all Australians now.

The very men who say that 
giving a woman a vote would 
degrade her, have not the 
slightest compunction about 
making her a drudge. They do 
not regard it as degrading 
for a woman to black a man’s 
boots. Oh, no! It is not 
degrading for her to scrub 
a floor or to be turned into 
a stuffy kitchen to cook for 
a man, or to be put into a 
factory where she will have to 
work nine or ten hours a day 
for a wretched pittance. None 
of these things will degrade 
a woman, but to give her a 
voice in the government of the 
country will degrade her!
Source: James Stewart Queensland, Australian 
Labor Party Queensland; Senate, 9 April 1902, 
p.11499
Only yesterday I heard a woman 
say that she did not think 
it would be safe to confer 
this right on women, because 
very dire things were likely 
to follow. It is alleged that 
women would be influenced by 
the clergy, by good-looking 
candidates and by young men.
Source: Thomas Glassey, Protectionist Party 
Queensland; Senate, 9 April 1902, p.11474
I believe that if we now decide to go in for womanhood 
suffrage it will tend to the vulgarization of women, 
and that none of us desires.
Source: Edward Pulsford, Free Trade Party, New South Wales; Senate, 9 April 1902, p. 11466
I am f irmly of the opinion that 
the extension of the franchise 
to women will cause men to 
take more interest in political 
matters, and to vote in larger 
numbers than they have done 
heretofore. The fact that 
wives and daughters in the 
home will be able to discuss 
political subjects which affect 
everyday life, will bring to 
the mind of the male portion 
of the community the necessity 
for recording their votes at 
election time.
Source: Sir William Lyne, Hume, Protectionist

The main ambition of a woman’s 
life should be to become the 
wife of an honourable and 
honest man.

I am a married woman living in Bay Street, Port Melbourne. I have six children. My husband is 
secretary to the Agricultural Implement Makers’ Union. I do not know what he earns but he 
gives me £2-10-0 [two pound, ten shillings] a week. This is not enough to keep the family going.
Source: Kate Russell, Testimony 1907 Ex parte HV McKay Harvester Case, Federal Court Arbitration and Conciliation. 
https://collections.museumvictoria.com.au/articles/15931
6	 Use a dictionary to write your own definition of ‘frugal comfort’. 
	
	
7	 What do you think a lifestyle of ‘frugal comfort’ would be in 1901? How about in 2020?

Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
5
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Origins of the  
Australian continent
Objectives
l To understand the concept of supercontinents
l To understand the concept of plate tectonics 
l To learn that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander 
peoples are the original inhabitants of Australia
Prior knowledge
l Students should have some familiarity with a 
map of the world and should be able to identify 
the continents.
Background
Pangea is the name given to the supercontinent 
that once contained all the continents of the earth. 
It began to break into Laurasia in the Northern 
Hemisphere and Gondwana in the Southern 
Hemisphere about 200 million years ago. Eventually, 
Laurasia and Gondwana broke up and the continents 
drifted apart very slowly to their present locations. 
 
In 1912 Alfred Wegener, a German meteorologist, 
presented his theory of continental drift and 
suggested that the continents had once fitted 
together. However, the idea was not supported 
by the scientists of the time. When evidence of 
plate tectonics was discovered, scientists revisited 
Wegener’s ideas. The theories of continental drift 
and plate tectonics were accepted about 50 years 
ago. These theories helped people understand the 
dynamism of the earth and why earthquakes and 
volcanic eruptions occur in specific areas.
The concept of geological time compared to 
human time needs to be explored in order to put the 
movement of the continents, and particularly the origin 
of Australia and its first inhabitants, into perspective. 
The melting of ice caps raised the sea level and 
formed Tasmania. It also changed what we now know 
as Central Australia and demonstrates that climate 
change has always occurred.
Starter activity
Brainstorm what the students know about how 
earth’s continents came to be arranged as they are. 
Students could visit: 
http://austhrutime.com/venerable.htm  
to research the origins of Indigenous Australia.
Discuss the difference between geological 
time – millions of years – compared with the first 
settlement of Australia about 60 000 years ago.  
Ask students for their ideas about how Indigenous 
people came to Australia, and where they came from.
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Origins of the Australian 
continent’, with the students. Given the continents 
that made up Gondwana, have students list the 
continents that must have made up Laurasia. Students 
could create a glossary in their workbooks, including 
supercontinent, Gondwana, Pangea and two more words 
of their own choice.
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘The 
continents’. They will need an atlas and the Resource 
sheet, ‘Origins of the Australian continent’.
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Sunda and 
Sahul’. Discuss the technique of using shading to show 
the amount of land there was during the Pleistocene 
era. You could explain that the sea level was lower due 
to lower temperatures which meant more water was 
stored in ice at the north and south of the earth. 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Origins’. 
Discuss the diagrams with the students, and point out 
the vast amounts of time between the eras shown. 
Students will complete a cloze activity about the 
theories of continental drift and plate tectonics. 
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Understanding our 
origins’, with the students. If they are keeping a glossary, 
students could add the terms Indigenous, archeologist 
and Sahul. To extend the activity, you could do a class 
Internet search for maps of early human migration and 
discuss what you find out. 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Origin 
match-up’, in which they will match definitions to key 
terms. Students may need to refer to the Resource and 
Activity sheets in the unit. 
extension activity
l  Use the Internet to find out where recent earthquakes 
have occurred and what has happened to the land 
and people.
l  Research the movement of Indigenous people from 
the north of Australia to the rest of the continent. 
Students will find that the coastal and tropical areas 
were colonised first, but eventually desert areas and 
the Tasmanian highlands were also colonised. 
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check them 
for inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
12
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – The Dreaming
Objectives 
l To understand the importance of mythology in 
prehistory
l To appreciate the significance of the Dreaming 
to the lives of Indigenous Australians
l To understand the relationship between the 
Dreaming stories and the Australian landscape
Prior knowledge
Students should have some experience of using 
storytelling to pass on information and ideas. 
Background
Stories played an important role in prehistoric times. 
Prehistory means ‘before written records’, and during 
this time people told stories to explain creation, 
the formation of physical features and natural 
phenomena like thunder, rainbows and stars. These 
stories taught people about traditions, culture and 
how they should live. They were told from generation 
to generation, and represented through dance, song 
and painting.  
Starter activity 
Ask students to imagine what life was like before 
people used written language. Ask questions such as: 
How do you think people communicated with each 
other? Could they communicate with people who 
lived far away? How could they remember or record 
important events? Tell students that we use the term 
‘prehistory’ to describe the time before people used 
written language. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Dreamtime, landscape 
and lifestyle’, with the students. Discuss the idea that 
the significance of the Dreaming forms the basis of 
Indigenous life, past and present, and is acknowledged 
in ‘Welcome to Country’ greetings at public ceremonies 
today. 
 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Understanding the Dreamtime’, where they summarise 
what they have learned from the Resource sheet, 
‘Dreamtime, landscape and lifestyle’. Discuss their 
answers as a class, and have students revise or add to 
their own answers to incorporate class ideas.  
 
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Creation 
story – the Rainbow Serpent’. Point out that many 
different tribes have their own versions of creation 
stories. Explain that this type of story tells of the creation 
of the landforms, vegetation and animals, as well as 
human society. Students will use vowels to complete the 
verbs in a version of the Rainbow Serpent story. 
 
Read the Resource sheet, ‘How were landforms 
created?’, with the students. Make sure students 
understand the meaning of the geological terms shown 
in bold. Explain that the Indigenous explanations are 
examples, and have been summarised. Students may 
wish to use the library or Internet to find out more 
about these explanations.  
 
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Finding landforms’, 
students will need an atlas and the Resource sheet, 
‘How were landforms created?’ They will complete a 
mapping task and comprehension questions about the 
information on the Resource sheet.
extension ideas
Research a detailed Indigenous explanation of the 
geographic features of Uluru at:
www.austhrutime.com/mythology_uluru.htm 
Other landforms such as Wave Rock, the Darling Scarp, 
Wilpena Pound, Arkaroola and the Grampians also have 
interesting stories to explain their existence. You can find 
information about these stories by selecting ‘Aboriginal 
Australia’ on the left menu of the www.austhrutime.com 
website, and scrolling down the list of articles.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check them 
for inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
18
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Land management
Objectives
l To understand the meaning of the term 
‘hunters and gatherers’
l To appreciate the need to look after the land
l To identify differences between Indigenous  
and European use of the land
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that there are different 
ways of using and caring for the land.
Background 
Early Indigenous Australians gained all the 
nourishment they needed while living sustainably 
on the land. The kinds of foods eaten by different 
tribes varied according to their location and the 
season. Dreamtime stories told them how to 
care for the land and its resources. Water became 
sacred, and in some areas wells were dug to tap 
underground supplies. Fire played an important 
part in warmth, cooking and hunting. Tribes would 
burn off areas at particular times of the year to 
encourage grass to grow. This provided a food 
source for the animals they hunted. The use of fire 
changed the vegetation, with fire-resistant species 
such as eucalypts and acacias becoming dominant.
Starter activity
Work with the class to define these key terms  
which are used throughout the unit: nomadic,  
semi-nomadic, cannibalism, sustainable, 
aromatic, legalised, hunters and gatherers.
Resource and Activity sheets
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Hunting 
and gathering’. Then discuss how this way of finding 
food compares with the way people obtain food 
today. Introduce the idea of a global food chain, and 
compare it with the local supply of food Indigenous 
people relied on. 
 
Have students read the Resource sheet, 
‘Indigenous methods of finding food’. Discuss 
the importance of sustainable use of resources to 
Indigenous Australians, and how sustainability relates 
to food supply today. For example, more people are 
growing their own vegetables and fruit, eat foods that 
are in season and are concerned about food miles 
and other environmental factors associated with food 
production. 
 
To complete the Activity sheets, ‘Finding food’ and 
‘Sustainable land use’, students will need to refer to the 
Resource sheet, ‘Indigenous methods of finding food’. 
 
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Food preparation’, with the 
students. Through this activity, students will gain an 
understanding of how Indigenous Australians ensured 
a constant food supply despite limited options for 
storing food. They will also learn about the availability 
today of some traditional foods.
 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Use of resources’, students 
complete a cloze exercise exploring the kinds of tools 
and equipment Indigenous Australians made, and how 
they were used. Students may need assistance with 
finding illustrations of the tools from online or library 
sources for the second part of the activity.  
extension ideas
l  Have students work in small groups to research 
the availability of bush tucker – in their local area, 
Australia-wide and internationally. Students could 
also compile a collection of recipes that use these 
ingredients.
l  Visit the Indigenous plant section of the local 
Botanical Gardens, and look for plants that can 
be used as food sources. Make sure the students 
understand that it is not safe to eat these plants unless 
they are taught how to prepare them correctly.

Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
25
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Indigenous art
Objectives
l To understand the significance of Indigenous 
art as a way to record thoughts, beliefs and 
early ways of life
l To appreciate the Indigenous connection to the 
Dreaming
l To realise that Indigenous art is found in other 
continents
l To understand that Indigenous Australian 
painting is considered the oldest continuous  
art form known today
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of the 
Dreaming and its importance to Indigenous life.
Background
Art using a variety of mediums has been a means 
of expression for people for thousands of years. 
Petroglyphs and rock art in caves, overhangs 
and on boulders have contributed to our current 
understanding of pre-history. Humans have always 
used art in its many forms to record information 
and ideas about spirituality, lifestyle and food 
sources. Some Indigenous paintings of sailing ships 
and buffalo hunting depict contact with European 
people. As Indigenous Australian art is so significant, 
both for its spirituality and the history it records, it 
is essential that it be respected and preserved for 
all Australians. Many modern Indigenous Australian 
artists continue to pass on stories of spirituality and 
country using traditional symbols and colour. 
Starter activity
Discuss why people create art, both today and in 
the past. Ensure students understand the distinction 
between pre-history (before use of a formal writing 
system) and history (when written records were 
kept). Explore what can be learned from early art and 
why it is important to our understanding of the past.
Resource and Activity sheets
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Rock art’. 
As they complete the cloze exercises they will gain an 
overview of Indigenous art in Australia. 
Read and discuss the Resource sheet, ‘Indigenous art 
styles’, with the class. Make sure students understand 
the meaning of each term shown in bold.  Then have 
students complete the questions on the Activity sheet, 
‘Different kinds of rock art’. To extend the activity, you 
could help students use the library or Internet to find 
examples of each type of art. 
Have students read the Resource sheet, ‘Threats 
to rock art’. Discuss the ways some is threatened, both 
intentionally and unintentionally. Then have studetns 
complete the Activity sheet, ‘How can we help protect 
rock art?’ Suggestions could include boardwalks to 
keep people on a given path, fences to keep people 
and animals at a safe distance from the art, car parks, 
fines, signs, educational and cautionary pamphlets 
and getting local Indigenous Australians or rangers 
oto remove nests and plants and keep the paintings 
drained. 
extension ideas 
l  Use a map of Australia to locate the art mentioned 
in the unit. Have the students suggest why the art is 
located in those places.
l  Visit a museum or art gallery to look at Indigenous 
art and artefacts. Alternatively, the website of the 
Australian Museum shows an extensive collection.

Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
31
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resources and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Contact with Indigenous 
Australians’, with the students. Explain to the students 
that there were also other visitors who are not listed in 
the table. Discuss the reasons why European nations 
wanted to expand their territory by colonising other 
places. Then have students complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Exploring Australia’. They will need to refer to the 
Resource sheet, ‘Discovering Australia’, to complete this 
activity. To extend the activity, you could have students 
list further factors that would be important to the first 
British settlers in sourcing food, water and shelter.
Have students read the Resource sheet, ‘Indigenous 
contact with Europeans (1)’. Discuss the concept 
of terra nullius and what happened to Australia’s 
original inhabitants as a result. Explain that this was the 
beginning of a radical change in lifestyle for Indigenous 
people. Then have students complete the Activity 
sheet, ‘Indigenous contact with Europeans (2)’. 
extension activity
l  Read about Governor Bourke’s 1835 Proclamation of 
Terra Nullius with the class at: 
http://www.migrationheritage.nsw.gov.au, then use 
the website’s search option with the key term: terra 
nullius. 
 
 The web page provides information about the 
social and political context in both Britain and 
Australia around the time of European occupation. 
It also discusses the fact that not all British people 
supported the way Australia was colonised. 
l  Lead a class discussion about the meaning of and 
connotations of the terms ‘invaded’ and ‘colonised’. 
Discuss whether the Europeans invaded or colonised 
Australia, and encourage students to give reasons for 
their opinions.
Teacher’s notes – European contact with  
Indigenous Australians
Objectives
l To understand that Europeans colonised other 
places because they wanted resources
l To appreciate the impact of colonisation on the 
Indigenous inhabitants of Australia
l To undertake mapping and interpretative tasks
Prior knowledge
Students should have some knowledge of 
migration to Australia from 1788 to the present, 
including the varying attitudes towards new arrivals.
Background
The first visitors to Northern Australia were the 
Macassans from modern-day Indonesia. They were 
searching for trepang (sea cucumbers) and traded 
with the Indigenous people. Signs of their presence 
remain in the Macassan words still present in 
Indigenous languages in the north. 
 
During the 16th to 18th centuries, Europeans 
explored the world in search of resources. Explorers 
who encountered the west coast of Australia found it 
inhospitable. 
 
Australia was the only British colony that was 
subject to the ruling of terra nullius (land belonging 
to no one), which contributed to the extreme 
disadvantage experienced by Indigenous Australians.
Starter activity
Discuss what students know about the first explorers 
to Australia, where they came from and why. Then 
develop a class list of different reasons why people 
want to come to Australia to live.

© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Customary law  
and Australian law
Objectives
l To understand that we need to have laws in 
order for society to function
l To appreciate Indigenous law
l To gain an understanding of the conflict 
between Indigenous law and Australian law 
Prior knowledge
Students should recognise right and wrong within 
a family, a community and a society and understand 
that there are consequences when the law is broken. 
Background 
Indigenous customary law came into being through 
the Dreaming, which determined the relationships 
between people and the land and became the basis 
of Indigenous culture. Laws were passed on through 
stories, song and dance. Different tribes had different 
specific laws. 
 
When laws relating to social interaction were 
broken, the elders and community members met 
with victims and offenders. They resolved the issues 
with mediation and determined the punishments, 
which were dealt out quickly – sometimes these 
punishments seem harsh and violent to Europeans. 
When laws relating to sacred matters were broken, 
the elders generally determined the punishment.
 
After European occupation, Australian law was 
written down and was the province of the judicial 
system, with resolution of crimes taking a long time 
and involving jail for some matters. This led to some 
Indigenous Australians being placed in custody and 
resulted in conflict between the cultures. 
 
Customary law is still practised today In some 
Indigenous communities. 
Starter activity
Lead a discussion about the reasons we have laws, 
how they are made and who administers them. 
Introduce the idea of more than one system of law 
operating within a region.
Activity sheets
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Customary law (1)’, with the 
students. Discuss the fact that different tribes had 
slightly different laws, and how this could affect people 
travelling across tribal boundaries. Students will 
complete sentence starters to summarise what they 
have read. You could tell students that current Australian 
state and territory boundaries were not finalised until 
after 1901 when they were created at the time of 
Federation. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘Customary law (2)’, students 
will explore further the traditions of Indigenous law. 
Students will need a dictionary to complete the first 
question. Point out that, unlike the Australian legal 
system, customary law did not separate religion, 
traditions and social rules. 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Comparing customary law and Australian law’. Students 
will learn about some traditional punishments in 
customary law, and compare the dispute resolution 
process with the Australian legal system. 
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Circle sentencing’, with 
the students. Sensitively discuss factors that could 
contribute to the higher percentage of Indigenous 
people in custody, such as cultural differences, lack of 
access to legal advice, and health and social issues such 
as remote locations and high unemployment rates. 
To complete the activity sheet, ‘Circle courts’, students 
will need an atlas or access to a mapping application, 
and a blank map of Australia. A map is provided on 
the CD-ROM in the Artwork > Unit 6 folder. Discuss the 
distribution of courts in relation to population centres.  
extension ideas 
Have students visit the website below to read more 
about circle sentencing and evaluate the importance 
and success of this process:
www.creativespirits.info/aboriginalculture/law/ 
circle-sentencing

© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012

Teacher’s notes – Health and opportunities
Objectives 
l To understand the need for good health, 
education, employment and income 
opportunities
l To recognise differences between Indigenous 
and non-Indigenous health and opportunities
l To appreciate ways to overcome this disparity, 
and to be aware of the variations between 
urban and remote Indigenous people 
l To improve mapping and graphing skills
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge required.
Background
Indigenous people had no resistance to diseases 
such as measles, smallpox and influenza, which were 
brought to Australia by European settlers. Traditional 
diets were well-balanced and contained little fat. 
Modern urban diets can be high in fat and sugar 
and low in fibre, which has been linked to obesity, 
diabetes and heart disease. These influences, plus 
other lifestyle factors acquired from Europeans 
such as smoking and alcohol consumption, have 
contributed to the high incidence of kidney and 
other diseases in Indigenous Australians. As a result, 
Indigenous life expectancy is not as high as it is for 
non-Indigenous people. 
 
In remote centres, lack of education reduces 
employment opportunities and contributes to social 
problems. 
 
Indigenous people in other countries such as 
New Zealand and the United States also experience 
disadvantages.
Starter activity
This is a sensitive topic that relates to low socio-economic 
areas as well as to Indigenous people. Ask students to 
think about the things they need to lead a healthy life 
and to have a successful future. Point out that not all the 
people who are disadvantaged are Indigenous, that not 
all Indigenous people are disadvantaged and that many 
Indigenous people have been successful in fields such as 
law, medicine, music and sport.
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Activity sheet, ‘What happened after European 
settlers arrived?’, with the students. Make sure students 
understand the meaning of the terms shown in bold. 
Students could work in pairs to answer the questions. 
 
Examine the graph on the Activity sheet, ‘Australian 
populations’, with the students. Make sure they 
understand how to read and interpret the graph. Discuss 
why these statistics are a valuable measure of Australian 
society.
 
Have students complete the mapping activity on the 
Activity sheet, ’Distance from major cities’. They will need 
an atlas or access to a mapping application, and a blank 
map of Australia. A map is provided on the CD-ROM in 
the Artwork > Unit 7 folder.   
 
Read and discuss the Resource sheet, ‘Opportunities in 
Australia (1)’, with the class. Then have them complete the 
Activity sheet, ‘Opportunities in Australia (2)’. You could 
extend this activity by exploring the website:  
http://www.indigenous.gov.au with the students, which 
provides further information about the government’s 
Closing the Gap policy. Students could list current 
government projects that are aimed at each category 
listed on the Activity sheet.
extension ideas
l  Students could research Indigenous people from 
another country and compare their treatment and 
outcomes with Australia’s Indigenous people; for 
example, the Maori people in New Zealand, the Inuit 
people in Canada or the Native Americans in the 
United States. 
l  Have students research the history of the White 
Australia Policy in Australia.

Teacher’s notes – Indigenous climate
Objectives
l To understand the difference between weather 
and climate
l To appreciate the importance of weather 
observations in Indigenous life
l To compare Indigenous and European 
interpretations of climatic events
l To learn how to graph and analyse data
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of  
the impact of weather on the clothes they wear, 
their sporting activities and decisions about  
holiday destinations.
Background
Weather and climate play a very important part in 
our decision making and daily lives. Early Indigenous 
Australians made detailed observations of weather, 
as their survival depended on knowledge of plant 
germination and growth, and the cycles of animals. 
This knowledge is linked to their sustainable use of 
the land and to the Dreaming. Indigenous Australians 
in different areas had many different experiences, 
as the size of the Australian continent and its 
topography created diverse conditions. Information 
was passed orally from generation to generation. 
Detailed accounts of the climate of northern 
Australia still exist, as well as for south-western 
Australia, the Grampians and the Sydney region. 
However, Indigenous climate information for the 
south-east of Australia has largely been lost due to 
European occupation.
The concept of four seasons, which the Europeans 
brought from the Northern Hemisphere, does not 
really fit with the Indigenous seasons. Up to six 
seasons have been identified in south-west Australia 
and the Northern Territory, and three in the centre  
of Australia.
Indigenous knowledge of weather and climate is 
now being recognised by the scientific community as a 
valuable contribution to the climate change discussion. 
Climate change is expected to contribute further to 
erosion of coastlines and rising sea levels. This may force 
some Torres Strait Island communities to move, causing 
physical and social disruption. 
Starter activity
Ask students to brainstorm why we need to know 
about the weather and climate. Discuss which 
occupations depend on this information. Explore the 
idea that today, a change in the weather doesn’t much 
affect whether people go to work or school not, where 
people live or what people eat. Why do the students 
think Indigenous Australians need to know about the 
weather? 
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Activity sheet, ‘The Australian Climate’, with 
the class. Students will rearrange sentence fragments 
and rewrite complete sentences about seasons from a 
European and Indigenous perspective. 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Climate 
statistics for Maningrida, NT’. Maningrida is a town in the 
Northern Territory on the north coast of Arnhem Land. 
Students will complete a climate graph by continuing to 
plot the data from a table. 
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Yolgnu seasons’, with 
the class. Students will learn about the features of the 
different Yolgnu seasons, and how this affects where the 
Yolgnu live and what they do. 
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Yolgnu and 
Maningrida seasons’, students will need the completed 
Activity sheet, ‘Climate statistics for Maningrida, NT’, 
and the Resource sheet, ‘Yolgnu seasons’. Students will 
answer questions to help them analyse and interpret 
the information provided.
extension ideas
Students could research climate data for their local area, 
or an area they would like to visit, and graph the data 
using the climate graph on the Activity sheet, ‘Climate 
statistics for Maningrida, NT’ as a model.

© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Indigenous tourism
Objectives
l To appreciate the importance of tourism for 
Indigenous people
l To understand the role of Indigenous people in 
Australian tourism
l To identify reasons that visitors take part in 
Indigenous tourism  
Prior knowledge
Students should understand that people  
visit places away from home for a variety  
of reasons.
Background
Indigenous tourists can be domestic – from 
Australia – or international. Indigenous tourists 
visit at least one Indigenous cultural site, art gallery,  
museum or Indigenous community.
The Australian Tourism Authority actively 
encourages and promotes Indigenous tourism, 
as do state government departments. Indigenous 
tourism allows overseas and Australian visitors to 
appreciate Australian Indigenous culture, past and 
present, as well as places of cultural significance. 
Indigenous tourism is run by Indigenous people 
or part-owned by Indigenous people. Alternatively, 
Indigenous people may be employed as guides and 
in other capacities. Indigenous tours have become 
more popular as people are becoming aware of the 
rich heritage and culture of Indigenous Australians. 
Their history of sustainable use of resources has also 
created interest. Indigenous tour operators provide 
a range of nature-based tourism events, cultural 
heritage and education programs on topics such 
as bush tucker, medicines, art and craft, as well as 
performances.
Starter activity
Create a class list of students’ tourism experiences. 
Classify them into categories, such as visiting family 
and friends, cultural, ecotourism, sport, relaxation  
and retail. Explain that Indigenous tourism is 
increasingly important in Australia, especially for 
Indigenous Australians employed in tourism who can 
showcase their culture and history. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Indigenous tourism (1)’, with 
the class. This provides examples of the great variety of 
activities and cultural experiences available. Discuss the 
different types of attractions tourists want to visit, and 
which attractions the students would most like to visit. 
Then have students complete the writing frame on the 
Activity sheet, ‘Indigenous tourism (2)’. 
 
To complete the mapping exercise on the Activity 
sheet, ‘Indigenous tourism – locations’, students will 
need the Resource sheet, ‘Indigenous tourism (1)’, and an 
atlas or mapping application. Some students may need 
assistance with developing a key for the different kinds 
of attractions.  
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Indigenous 
tourism visitors’. Discuss what the graph shows – 
numbers of International and domestic tourism 
visitors – and how to read the data presented. Explain 
that while these visitors do not exclusively look for 
Indigenous experiences, they include at least one 
in their plans. Note that the decreasing numbers of 
tourists largely reflects the effects of the global financial 
crisis and the increasing value of the Australian dollar. 
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Being a responsible 
tourist’, with the class, which provides tips about being 
respectful at Indigenous tourism attractions. Students 
will use this information to help them explain why it is 
important for tourists to respect Indigenous culture.  
extension ideas
Have students choose a region such as the Kimberley, 
Uluru or Kadadu, and research a journey through the 
region with an Indigenous guide. They could create an 
itinerary and a visual diary to record the things they 
would expect to see.

Teacher’s notes – Native title
Objectives 
l To understand the reasons for native title and 
Indigenous land use agreements 
l To create and analyse a graph
l To learn about and empathise with the 
traditional values of Indigenous Australians
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of what 
belonging to a family or community means. 
They should also be aware that traditions can be 
expressed in many ways.
Background
When Australia was occupied by the Europeans, 
Indigenous people were subjected to dispossession 
of their lands and a lack of understanding of their 
culture. The Indigenous population was severely 
diminished by introduced diseases. There were 
many instances of conflict between Indigenous 
people and European settlers. In the late 19th and 
early 20th centuries, many Indigenous people 
were forced to live on missions and reserves. The 
European approach to assimilation resulted in 
the stolen generations. It was not until 1967 that 
Indigenous people were counted in the national 
census. 
 
In 1992, after ten years of hard work by Eddie 
Mabo and his friends, native title was recognised.  
However, it can be difficult to prove in the courts. 
 
Indigenous land use agreements are a voluntary 
agreement between traditional owners and people 
who want to use the land. These agreements don’t 
require native title, but can help to support a native 
title claim. They are a way for people to work out 
a mutually beneficial way of managing and/or 
developing an area. Common land uses include 
pastoral grazing and mining. 
Starter activity
Discuss native title with the students, and find out what 
they know or think they know about it. In particular, 
explore which categories of land the students think can 
be subject to native title – such as houses, farms, and 
national parks. (Many people are unaware that native 
title can only apply to government-owned land, national 
parks, public land and pastoral leases.) Record their ideas 
in a chart or mind map for later review.
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘History of native title’, with the 
students. Make sure students understand that Mabo’s 
victory was important to more people than those in the 
Murray Islands – it meant that other Indigenous people 
could also apply for native title for their own land. On the 
Activity sheet, ‘About native title’, students will answer 
questions relating to the information of the Resource 
sheet.
Have students complete the cloze activity on the 
Activity sheet, ‘Indigenous land use agreements’. Tell the 
students that the areas covered by ILUAs are private and 
must be respected, which is why people need permits 
to enter places such as Uluru. It may be useful to discuss 
the similarities and differences between ILUAs and 
native title before students answer the second question. 
extension ideas
l  Review the chart from the discussion in the starter 
activity. Work with the students to correct and add to 
it as needed. 
l  Students could research the life and work of Eddie 
Mabo, and prepare a report outlining why the Mabo 
case is so important. 
l  The Indigenous Land Corporation is an independent 
statutory authority of the federal government which 
helps Indigenous people to buy and manage land. 
Students could explore their website and prepare a 
report outlining what they do, and what has been 
achieved: http://www.ilc.gov.au

Resource sheet – Origins of the  
Australian continent
Origins of the Australian continent
It is hard to imagine now, but Australia was once part of a huge supercontinent named 
Gondwana which existed mostly in the southern hemisphere. Before that, Gondwana 
was part of Pangea (Greek for ‘all lands’), a massive supercontinent made up of all the 
continents we know now. 
Pangea began splitting into Gondwana and Laurasia – another supercontinent – about 
200 million years ago.  Gondwana was enormous, made up of present-day Africa, South 
America, India, Australia and Antarctica.
How do we know? Some of the same kinds of rocks and fossils are found across the 
modern land masses that made up Gondwana, but not anywhere else. 
In 1861, an Austrian geologist named Eduard Suess first suggested the theory that 
Gondwana had existed. Suess realised that the fossil plant Glossopteris (a fern-like tree) 
could be found in all the land masses of the former Gondwana, and decided that this 
meant these lands were once joined together. Suess named Gondwana after a district in 
India where the fossil plant was found.

Activity sheet – Origins of the  
Australian continent 
Sunda and Sahul
Has Australia looked the same since it began to drift north from Antarctica about  
96 million years ago?
During the geological era known as the Pleistocene (from 2.5 million to 12 000 years 
ago), the sea level was up to 150 metres lower than it is today. The shaded area on the 
map shows what the land looked like then. Tasmania was still joined to the mainland of 
Australia, which was joined to New Guinea. This land mass was known as Sahul. Sahul was 
separated from Sunda, another land mass, by the Sunda Strait. 
+ 1 List the countries that now make up the original Sunda and Sahul.
 
________________________________________________________________________
 
________________________________________________________________________
 
________________________________________________________________________
2 Mark each statement as true or false.

Resource sheet – Origins of the  
Australian continent 
Understanding our origins
 
●It is believed that Australia’s Indigenous people came to Australia 
through South-East Asia. The first human migration was probably 
when Australia was part of the Sahul land mass. However, there 
were still large areas of water, so people needed boats or rafts to 
get from Sunda to Sahul. These people may have come via  
modern-day Malaysia.
 
●Indigenous Australians are the original inhabitants of Australia 
and its nearby islands. Indigenous people who live on the 
Australian mainland, Tasmania and islands such as Flinders Island 
and King Island are often called ‘Aboriginal’. The Indigenous 
people who inhabit islands near Cape York are called Torres  
Strait Islanders.
 
●The oldest Aboriginal remains were those of Mungo Man, found 
near Lake Mungo in New South Wales. Mungo Man is believed to 
be about 50 000 years old.
 
●Humans reached Tasmania about 40 000 years ago by travelling 
across a land bridge from the mainland. About 12 000 years ago, 
the glacial ice melted and the sea level rose to present-day levels, 
creating Bass Strait. The people in Tasmania were isolated from the 
mainland until European settlers arrived.

Achieve!
Resource sheet – The Dreaming
Dreamtime, landscape and lifestyle 
 
●For thousands of years, Indigenous Australians have told stories to pass 
their culture from generation to generation. Dreaming stories told 
Indigenous Australians about how to live their lives.
 
●In the Dreaming stories, there are close links between the physical, 
human and spiritual worlds. The stories are told through song, dance and 
painting, as well as speaking.
 
●The Dreaming relates to the time of creation, when the Spirit Ancestors 
came out of the earth. They moved across the land and created sacred 
places. They made important features of the landscape like mountains, 
rivers, lakes and waterholes. They made flora and fauna, and the laws of 
the landscape too. Their movements are recorded in Dreaming Tracks, 
which join the sites the Ancestral Beings passed. 
 
●Dreaming stories tell about the Indigenous culture and customs, and the 
laws of the community. They also explain how people should behave and 
the consequences of disobedience, including punishments.
 
●In the stories, living sustainably and caring for the land and its features, 
plants and animals, are an important part of the traditions and culture.
 
●Dreaming stories also contain practical information such as where food 
grows and in which season it ripens. Indigenous people believe that each 
type of food was created by the Spirit Ancestors.
 
●Totems are objects of nature which become family emblems. They are 
given to people in certain areas. Some people are given personal totems 
at birth. Totems are important in song and dance.

Stories provided Indigenous people with 
a map of the land and knowledge of food

There are a number of Dreaming creation

The Rainbow Serpent is always associated

properly respected, it could turn people into rocks, mountains and other landforms.

Resource sheet – The Dreaming
How were landforms created? 
Indigenous explanation
Geological explanation
Uluru, Northern Territory
The south side resulted from a battle between 
the Liru, the poisonous snakes, and the Kunia, 
the carpet snakes. 
Hard sandstone rock was laid down under 
the sea millions of years ago. The surrounding 
softer material has been worn away over time, 
leaving the monolith, Uluru.
Kandimal (Wolfe Creek Crater), Western Australia
Two Rainbow Snakes moved across the 
country, carving the paths of Stuart Creek 
and Wolfe Creek. The crater formed where the 
snakes came out of the earth.
Wolfe Creek Crater is the second biggest 
meteorite crater in the world. The meteorite 
hit the earth 2 million years ago.
Lake Eyre, South Australia 
Wikuda, a young boy, chased a white kangaroo 
and speared it. Wikuda put the skin down east 
of Anna Creek. The skin became Lake Eyre.
Once covered by the sea, Lake Eyre is now 15 
metres below sea level and salty. The wind has 
removed the sand. Now water flows in from 
the Diamantina River and Cooper Creek. 
Buda-dji (Barron Gorge), Queensland
Buda-dji, shaped like a carpet snake, carved 
out the famous gorge. 
Formed by the River Barron cutting down 
through the escarpment on its path to 
the sea.
Murray River, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia
Pondi the Murray cod was chased by the 
Ngurenderi the hunter from New South Wales 
to Lake Alexandrina, making the bends and 
banks of the river as he dodged and weaved 
his way.
The source of the river is a spring near  
Mt Kosciuszko. The river collects water from 
the tributaries as it flow to the sea through 
the mouth of the river, in South Australia.
The Three Sisters, New South Wales
Three sisters, Meenhi, Wimlah and Gunnedoo, 
were turned to stone as punishment for 
meeting three men they were not supposed 
to see. 
Sand was deposited in the sea where it 
hardened into sandstone. The land was 
uplifted and the sandstone was worn away by 
rain and wind, leaving the three rocks.

Achieve!
Indigenous Australians were very skilful hunters and gatherers.  
The types of foods they ate varied according to where they lived  
– in deserts, tropical rainforests or mountains, along the coast or near 
rivers. Food sources also varied according to the seasons.
The traditional Indigenous diet has all the vitamins and minerals 
that people need. Indigenous people have a detailed knowledge of the foods in their 
area, and only collected or hunted what they needed and what was in season.
Indigenous Australians ate many different types of foods. If a food they usually ate 
wasn’t available, for example during a drought, they simply ate something else, or 
moved to a different part of their tribal area. 
The locations of waterholes were passed down from generation to generation.  
Many of these sites, such as those at Uluru, became sacred.

© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Land management
Indigenous methods of finding food
Indigenous people traditionally led a nomadic life inland and a semi-nomadic life near 
the coast and rivers. They knew how to care for the land, and only took what they needed 
so that their land use was sustainable.
Men and women spent most of the day collecting food. Women dug up yams and 
other roots as well as collecting seeds. Women and children collected ants, honey ants and 
witchetty grubs and killed small animals with digging sticks. Men hunted in groups when 
catching kangaroos and emus, and hunted alone to catch small animals like possums, 
snakes and birds.
People along rivers and near the coast caught fish. There is a fish trap at Brewarrina in 
New South Wales that is 40 000 years old, and is still being used. Coastal tribes collected 
oysters, mussels and crabs, which are a good source of energy.
When hunting, people used fire to scare out animals so they could kill them. People 
also set fire to certain areas at particular times of year to encourage grass to grow. This 
helped to feed the animals and sustain their numbers, so that there were enough for 
people to hunt. Over time, fire has changed the environment by encouraging fire-resistant 
plants to grow.
If a person’s totem was a particular bird, animal or plant, they would not kill or eat that 
thing, as this was regarded as cannibalism.
Water was sourced from rivers and waterholes. When these dried up, tribes had to 
move in search of more water.
At times, tribes would meet to socialise through feasting, perform ceremonies and 
trade with each other. Often it was the harvesting of a particular food source that brought 
people together. For example, when Bogong moths migrated to the Snowy Mountains 
during summer, tribes from around the area would meet and feast on the roasted moths. 
The bunya nut festival in the Bunya Mountains, Queensland, is another example.

+ 1 Cross out the incorrect word inside each set of brackets.
A lot of food was eaten (raw / rawe) by Indigenous Australians. Meat was cooked 
quickly on hot (coals / koles), mostly to remove feathers and fur, but it was not cooked 
all the way through. Some (cedes / seeds) were ground between stones to make flour, 
which could be made into cakes to be cooked on the fire or in stone ovens. Food 
could not be (storred / stored), but it was preserved in a few places. For example, 
(fish / fisch) were smoked in hollow gum trees along the lower River Murray and strips of 
(kangeroo / kangaroo) were sun-dried in some central (desert / dessert) areas.
In the 1970s, non-Indigenous Australians began to understand the use of native foods. 
Gradually kangaroo meat was legalised for sale, and then emu and crocodile (meet / meat). 
Aromatic plants like lemon myrtle and fruits and nuts such as quandong, Paterson’s plum 
and macadamia nuts, have become available. Some restaurants specialise in ‘bush tucker’ 
while others offer (native / natif) foods on their menus.

© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Indigenous art 
Indigenous art styles
 
●Rock art varied throughout Australia as Dreaming stories and food supplies differed 
from place to place. Some sites displayed the lives of the people, with drawings 
showing fish, animals, weapons and animal tracks as well as mythical beings. The 
heritage-listed Dampier Archipelago in Western Australia has many collections of 
rock art, as does Arnhem Land in the Northern Territory.
 
●Rock engravings or petroglyphs (petro meaning ‘rock’ and glyph meaning ‘symbol’) 
were carved into large flat sandstones by rubbing designs into them with a hard 
stone. The Olary region of South Australia has excellent examples – designs there 
include fish and crocodile heads.
 
●Rock paintings were made in shelters like caves. People used ochre to make red, 
yellow kaolin to make white, and charcoal to make black. 
 
●Hand painting was very common, especially in the southern parts of Australia. 
Artists placed one hand on the surface of a cave or rock and blew ochre over 
it, leaving the outline. Examples of this can be seen in the Cave of Hands in the 
northern Grampians.
 
●In Arnhem Land, some paintings show the internal organs of humans and animals. 
This style is known as X-ray art.
 
●Dot painting began in the Central and Western desert. Artists used ochre, sand, 
blood, charcoal, small rocks, flowers, feathers and seeds to create the art on ground 
for ceremonial events. The paintings showed symbols of the landscape as well as 
Dreaming stories. The meanings of the symbols varied according to the tribe and the 
region where they were painted. In 1972, the community at Papunya, 240 kilometres 
north-west of Alice Springs, transferred the method to modern canvas using acrylic 
paints. Sacred objects were not allowed to be shown on modern paintings. 
 
●For ceremonial occasions, Indigenous people painted their faces, arms and upper 
bodies with symbols, often relating to totems.

Threats to rock art
Rock art is important to Indigenous Australians as it records their history and culture. 
It must be preserved so that future generations of Australians can understand it and learn 
from it. In the past, Indigenous Australians regrooved and repainted rock art to preserve it. 
Cave art at Yuendumu in the Northern Territory cave art has recently been restored.  
Here are some of the threats to rock art:
 
l Moisture, fire  
and dust can  
cause damage  
to rock art.
 
l Animals such  
as wild buffalo  
in the Northern  
Territory rub  
against paintings  
and wear them away.
 
l Birds and insects 
like mud wasps 
build nests on  
rock walls.
 
l Fungi and lichen can  
grow over paintings,  
especially in damp,  
tropical areas.
 
l Non-Indigenous 
people can 
damage the rock 
art by painting 
the grooves with 
white paint to try 
to preserve it; for example,  
near Bondi Beach.
 
l In Esperance, Western  
Australia, graffiti has  
been scratched into  
paintings that are  
thousands of  
years old.
 
l Pollution in the 
atmosphere from  
cars and factories  
eats away the  
colours and  
patterns.
 
l Tourists 
treading on 
rock art can 
wear it away.

Resource sheet – European contact with  
Indigenous Australians
Indigenous contact with Europeans (1)
The arrival of Captain Arthur Phillip from England with the First 
Fleet in 1788 changed the lives of Indigenous people forever. It took 
about 100 years for the impact of European occupation to reach the 
centre of Australia. 
It is thought that there were about 750 000 Indigenous 
Australians when European settlers arrived. At first, the Indigenous 
Australians and the Europeans were curious about each other and 
treated each other with respect. However, this soon changed as the 
two groups could not understanding each other’s culture.
Soon after the arrival of the colonists, diseases such as smallpox, 
influenza and measles spread throughout the Indigenous people, 
who had no immunity to them. This resulted in many deaths.
The land was not developed in a way the Europeans understood 
– there were no houses, fences or farmed animals. They took over the 
land, especially around waterholes and areas with fertile soil. They 
built towns and tried to farm the land the way people did in England.
The Europeans did not understand the Indigenous relationship 
with the land or their sustainable use of resources. Many conflicts 
occurred when Indigenous Australians resisted being pushed off 
their land. 
The colonisation of Australia was based on the legal concept 
of terra nullius, which means ‘land of no one’. In 1835, the British 
government officially declared Australia to be terra nullius.

© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Indigenous Australians had developed a complex system of law thousands of years 
before Europeans came to Australia. Customary Indigenous law is based on beliefs, 
culture and the land, which all came from the Dreaming. Laws were passed down 
through generations using stories, song and dance. 
Each tribe has their own system of law, so while there are many similarities between 
tribes, there are also many variations. Tribal areas were largely defined by language 
groups, although rivers and other natural features may have formed boundaries. In 
1788, there were at least 250 tribal areas. Many tribes shared common areas which 
were used for ceremonies. People asked permission of neighbouring tribes if they 
wanted to travel through their lands.

Customary law (2)
The Dreaming provides Indigenous Australians with much more than a set of rules or 
laws to follow. The Dreaming is the basis for Indigenous lore – a body of knowledge, 
beliefs, customs and traditions. Rules for how to behave (customary law), are a part of 
Indigenous lore. Indigenous lore sets out clear rules for the way society should function, 
including how everyone should behave, ceremonial relationships and who can marry.
Australian Law refers to the justice system introduced to Australia by the British 
colonists. This legal system was originally the same as the one in England. 
In remote parts of Australia, customary law is still practised and this can come into 
conflict with the Australian legal system.
+ 1  Write the terms in bold in the information above in your workbooks.  
Use a dictionary and work with a partner to write a definition for each one.

There are no courts or __ __ __ __ sentences in customary law, but 
there are a variety of __ __ __ __ __ __ __ __ __ __ __. A problem

sorted out by community members, including the offender and the

Elders were always involved in offences against sacred __ __ __. These

Comparing customary law  
and Australian law
In customary law, there are different punishments for different offences. Each tribe had its 
own system of crimes and punishments.
In the past, death through spearing or sorcery might be the consequence of breaking 
sacred law. 
Spearing in the thigh could be used as payback for crimes such as murder, personal injury 
or adultery. In some tribes, people were banished for breaking laws. 
Shaming was used to punish offences like neglecting family members and insulting 
behaviour.

41
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
In Australia there is a higher percentage of Indigenous Australians in jail than  
non-Indigenous Australians. In 2011, Indigenous people made up 26% of Australia’s 
prison population but only 2.5% of the total population. In the Northern Territory,  
83% of the prison population is Indigenous. 
One strategy being used in New South Wales to try and reduce the number of 
Indigenous people in jail is circle sentencing. The ‘circle’ consists of four Indigenous 
elders, the offender, the victim, a defence lawyer and a magistrate. They try to work 
out a fair sentence for the offender that does not include going to jail. They talk about 
the background of the offender and the situation, and how the crime has affected the 
victim and the community. Often the sentence involves community work. People can 
only use circle sentencing if they plead guilty. 
There are similar courts with different names in other states and territories. The 
sentences given are strict, but the process helps to reduce the number of people who  
re-offend.

Achieve!   Geography – indigenous contexts
44
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
When Europeans settled Australia in 1788, life for Indigenous people was changed 
forever. Indigenous people were driven inland as the new settlers took over coastal 
land for farming. Indigenous Australians did not have any resistance to European 
diseases like influenza and smallpox, so many died – causing the population to drop, 
especially near the coast. Over time, the Indigenous people’s way of life was changed 
and their diet altered, especially with the introduction of sugar and flour. This led to an 
increase in the rate of medical problems like diabetes, kidney disease, heart disease, 
and eye and ear problems. It took much longer for Indigenous people in inland 
regions to be affected by new settlers looking for land. 
 
From the end of the 19th century until the 1970s, many children were taken from 
their families by government officials and placed in institutions. It was believed that 
this would help them to fit into European society. This caused significant and lasting 
damage to the children, their families and their tribes. 
Overall, Australia has a very high standard of living. But there are distinct 
differences in standard of living between some Indigenous and non-Indigenous 
people.

The Australian climate
There are a variety of different climates within Australia. These different climates are due 
to factors such as latitude (how close you are to the equator), altitude (height above sea 
level) and distance from the coast. Indigenous Australians closely observe the weather as it 
is critical to their food supply, their shelter and their links to the land. Europeans introduced 
their ideas of four distinct seasons, but most parts of Australia do not fit this classification  
of climate.

Resource sheet – Native title
History of native title
The occupation of Australia in 1788 by the British was based on the principle 
of terra nullius, which means ‘land belonging to no one’. At the time, British law 
allowed the settlement of ‘uninhabited or barbarous country’. They did not 
understand the Indigenous way of occupying, using and connecting to the 
land. The British took over the land, especially around waterholes and areas 
with fertile soil. They built towns and tried to farm the land the way people did 
in Britain.
 
In 1982, Eddie Mabo argued that the Queensland government should 
recognise that Indigenous people on the Murray Islands, his original home in 
the Torres Strait, already had a system of law and customary use of the land 
at the time of British occupation. In June 1992, five months after Mabo’s death, 
the High Court of Australia decided that Mabo was right. Native title was 
recognised and this overturned the idea of terra nullius.
Native title means that Australian law recognises some Aboriginal and 
Torres Strait Islanders’ rights to their land and waters, based on their laws 
and customs. In order to gain native title, Indigenous people have to prove an 
unbroken connection to their land and waters.
Native title can only be gained on Crown land (government-owned land), 
national parks, public land and pastoral leases, and it cannot be sold. Native 
title allows Indigenous people to live in the area, camp, carry out traditional 
ceremonies, hunt, fish and gather food, as well as visit and protect important 
sites. Native title can only be gained through the courts.

Teacher’s notes – Sustainable energy
Objectives
● To understand the concept of sustainability
● To recognise the need for sustainability
● To identify renewable and non-renewable 
resources
● To learn how sustainable energy can assist 
with climate change and the health of the 
environment
Prior knowledge
● Students should have some understanding of 
resources and the fact that they can be used up, 
especially as the population grows. They should 
also know that the use of fossil fuels has an 
impact on climate change, air quality and health, 
and that is is possible to generate power from 
renewable energy sources. 
Background
There has been much discussion regarding the 
need to use renewable energy as our understanding 
of  the effects of burning fossil fuels increases, 
and our fossil fuel supplies decrease. However, all 
forms of renewable energy have advantages and 
disadvantages. Wind power, solar power, tidal power, 
geothermal energy and biomass are regarded as 
green energy sources. Hydro-electric power and 
nuclear power are considered sustainable energy 
sources by some people. 
Starter activity 
Compile a class list of all the ways students use 
power. Then introduce the idea that power is also 
used to produce and distribute everything they buy. 
Add to the list the things the students buy regularly. 
Resource and activity sheets 
Provide students with the Activity sheet, 
Sustainability’. Read the introduction and speech 
bubbles with the students. Encourage them to 
suggest further examples of sustainability, then 
discuss what sustainability is. Students will work in 
pairs to write their own definitions for sustainability. 
 
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Why do we need 
sustainable energy?’, with the students. For each fossil 
fuel, point out the number of years it is expected 
to last at current rates of consumption. Encourage 
students to suggest reasons why countries still use 
fossil fuels. Introduce the idea that it is cheaper in 
terms of money for countries to continue using fossil 
fuels than to invest in the research, technology and 
infrastructure need to use renewable energy sources.  
 
Ask students to complete the Activity sheet, ‘Global 
supplies of fossil fuels’. They will need a copy of the 
Resource sheet, ‘Why do we need sustainable energy?’, 
an atlas or access to an Internet map search, and a blank 
world map. A map is provided on the CD-ROM in the 
Artwork > Unit 1 folder. Some students may need 
assistance with developing an appropriate key. When 
they have completed the mapping activity, students 
answer questions about the regions that have large 
and small fossil fuel reserves. 
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Renewable and non-
renewable resources’ with the students. Ensure students 
understand the meaning of ‘resource’ and that resources 
can be renewable or non-renewable. Introduce the idea 
that while some resources are renewable, they can also 
be scarce, like bananas after a cyclone in Queensland. 
Also, some resources require sound environmental 
management to be used sustainably; for example, fish 
supplies can be unsustainable due to human activities 
such as ocean pollution and overfishing. Students 
could use the Internet to check their answers to the last 
question.
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Reducing 
energy use’. Some students might prefer to work in pairs. 
You could compile a class list of their ideas for reducing 
energy use. .
extension idea
●  Take a tour of the school, and have the students note 
ideas for reducing energy use. If possible, choose 
several ideas and develop a plan to implement them.

Teacher’s notes – Wave power
Objectives 
● To learn about wave power
● To consider the advantages and disadvantages 
of using wave power, now and in the future
● To consider the effects of technological 
development on power generation
Prior knowledge
Students should have an understanding of the  
need to use clean, renewable energy, now and in 
the future.
Background
The idea of using wave power has been around for 
at least 200 years. The technology is now available 
and has been proven to be a viable source of power, 
although there is concern about the longevity of 
the equipment. As with all new technology, the 
cost of research and development and the initial 
infrastructure costs are significant factors. However, 
as fossil-fuel-generated power becomes more 
expensive and society focuses on reducing carbon 
emissions, this method of power generation will 
become more affordable. 
 
Australia is well placed to utilise wave power 
with its vast coastline and huge oceans washing the 
shores. Wave power sites include Geraldton in the 
west, along the south coast, in Tasmania and on the 
northern coast of New South Wales. 
 
In the Asia Pacific, Japan is seeking safer 
alternatives to nuclear power and the government 
is investigating ways to use their 4.47 million square 
kilometres of territorial waters for power generation. 
Starter activity
Have students share their experiences of the ocean. 
Guide the discussion to bring out the ideas that waves 
are continuous, and they are powerful. 
Raise the idea of using the power of the ocean to 
generate electricity. Encourage students to suggest how 
they think this could work.
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘What is wave power?’, with the 
students. You could provide images of coastal features 
such as the 12 Apostles on the Victorian south coast 
to extend the idea of waves shaping coastlines over 
time. Tell the students that wave energy has also been 
responsible for many shipwrecks, both near coasts 
and out at sea. Look carefully at the diagram showing 
how wave power is harnessed. Point out that as well as 
harnessing energy, this technology can supply another 
scarce resource – fresh water. 
 
Have students complete the cloze exercise on the 
Activity sheet, ‘Generating power’.  Encourage them to 
consider the role of technology in providing renewable 
energy. 
 
Provide students with the Resource sheet, ‘Opinions 
about wave power’. Take the opportunity to discuss 
the difference between an opinion and a fact. Students 
could decide what their own opinions are about wave 
power. 
 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Advantages and 
disadvantages’, students summarise what they have 
learned about wave power, and categorise their 
knowledge into advantages and disadvantages. 
Students may find it useful to refer to the Resource 
sheets, ‘What is wave power?’ and ‘Opinions about wave 
power’. Then students will write a persuasive letter to an 
electricity supply company.  
extension idea
● Students could design a survey to find out what 
people know about wave power. They could also find 
out whether people think it is a good idea or not, and 
the reasons for their opinions.

Teacher’s notes – Geothermal energy
Objectives 
● To learn about geothermal energy
● To understand the difference between  
natural geothermal energy and  
engineered geothermal energy
● To appreciate the advantages and difficulties 
associated with geothermal energy
Prior knowledge
Students should understand that the earth has 
layers and the earth’s core is molten. They  
should be aware that erupting volcanoes spew  
out hot lava. 
Background
In the past, geothermal energy was only harnessed 
in volcanic regions where naturally occurring hot 
water and steam came to the surface. For centuries 
Japan and New Zealand have used this resource for 
cooking. More recently it has been used to  generate 
electricity and pipe steam to heat houses, and for 
tourism attractions.
Engineered thermal energy is a renewable 
resource capable of producing base load (24 hours 
per day) energy. It does not release carbon dioxide 
into the atmosphere. No waste is produced during 
the process. The environmental impact is minimal – 
drill holes, pipelines and power plants. 
Potentially, geothermal energy could produce 
enough energy to supply Australia for a very long 
time. However, the necessary infrastructure of 
powerlines is not currently in place and would be 
very expensive. Small earthquakes can occur as a 
result of the drilling – one plant in Switzerland had 
to be shut down after earthquakes caused damage 
to buildings. Obtaining the information needed to 
map suitable sites is also very expensive.
Starter activity
Before class, conduct an Internet image search or 
YouTube search for ‘geothermal mud pools’. Select 
images and /or movies to show the class. Display 
them, and ask students to explain what that think 
is happening. Some students may have visited the 
mud pools in Rotorua, New Zealand. 
Tell the students that this is an example of heat and 
steam coming from within the earth’s surface. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘What is geothermal power?’, 
with the students. Ensure the students are familiar with 
the meaning of each word shown in bold. Discuss the 
difference between natural geothermal energy and 
engineered geothermal energy. To extend the activity, 
you could watch the Internet video about Paralana 
geothermal plant (Internet search terms: ‘Paralana 
geothermal plant’).
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Hot rocks’. 
Review the concept of the layers of the earth. You could 
use the analogy of an egg: the earth’s crust is like the 
shell of the egg, the mantle is like the egg white and 
the core is like the egg yolk. Allow time for students to 
practise and revise their verbal explanations for how 
geothermal power is generated. This particular diagram 
shows a binary cycle geothermal power plant – further 
information about how it works is readily available on 
the Internet. 
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Advantages and 
disadvantages’, with the students. Discuss the items in 
the lists and ensure students understand why each one 
is either an advantage or a disadvantage. You could 
work with the class to compare these advantages and 
disadvantages to those of another type of energy 
source, such as coal, wave or solar. 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Hot 
rock energy production’. They may need to refer to 
the Resource sheets, ‘What is geothermal power?’ 
and ‘Advantages and disadvantages’. After they have 
completed the activity, students could work in small 
groups to discuss their ideas for the second section. 
extension idea
●  Have the students cut out or draw the diagram 
from the Activity sheet, ‘Hot rocks’. Challenge them 
to label the diagram to explain what is happening 
and how it works. Students may like to work in 
pairs. The diagram shows a binary cycle geothermal 
power plant. Further information about the use and 
function of these power plants is readily available on 
the Internet.

Teacher’s notes – Wind power
Objectives 
● To learn about wind power and its advantages 
and disadvantages
● To learn how and where wind power can  
be generated
● To understand different opinions about  
wind farms
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that wind is an integral 
part of weather and climate, and be able to give 
examples of the use of wind in daily life.
Background
As the demand for energy increases with a growing 
global population, fossil fuel resources are dwindling. 
Increased energy consumption means carbon 
dioxide and other greenhouse gas emissions are 
contributing to climate change. In an effort to reduce 
greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy sources 
such as wind are being explored. Governments 
are setting targets to encourage the use of clean, 
renewable energy such as wind power, although it 
cannot generate a base load (24-hour) supply.
Starter activity
Introduce the concept of the wind. Discuss with 
the students what it is, and how people harness 
the power of the wind. As well as its potential to 
generate energy, encourage students to consider its 
role in sailing, in sports such as hang gliding and kite 
surfing, and its effect of different kinds of aircraft. 
Point out that people cannot control the wind, and 
discuss its potential to cause damage; for example, 
storms and cyclones and spreading bushfires.
Activity sheets
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Wind power’. 
Students will need an atlas, a blank map of Australia 
and Internet access to complete this activity. A map 
is provided on the CD-ROM in the Artwork > Unit 4 
folder. Before students begin the activity, make sure 
they understand the meaning of each term in bold. 
When they have finished, discuss the distribution of 
the wind farms and any patterns in the kinds of places 
they are located. To extend the activity, students could 
research global use of wind power. Countries such as 
New Zealand and China use wind-generated power. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘Wind power and sustainability’, 
students will extend their knowledge about wind 
power, and the importance of using renewable energy.
The Activity sheet, ‘Carbon dioxide emissions’, 
provides a graph of carbon dioxide emissions per 
person in Australia. Students are guided through the 
process of analysing the graph, then explaining what 
this means in terms of future energy use. 
On the Activity sheet, ‘How wind turbines work’, 
students will gain an understanding of how wind 
power is generated by completing the description of 
how each part works.
The Activity sheet, ‘Current use of wind power’, 
provides information about wind power, and presents 
a pie graph showing the capacity for wind power 
electricity generation in Australia, for each state and 
territory. Have the students consider the proportions 
in terms of physical size and population of each state, 
and other natural resources it may be more efficient 
to harness. Students will answer questions about the 
graph, and list advantages and disadvantages of wind 
power. 
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Opinions about wind farms’, 
with the class, and ensure they understand the meaning 
of each term in bold. Then students write their own 
opinions about wind farms. Encourage them to provide 
reasons for their opinions. 
extension idea 
●  Ask students to design a survey to find out what 
people know about wind farms, and their opinions 
on whether wind farms are a good idea or not.
