Teacher’s notes – Solar energy
Objectives 
● To learn about solar energy
● To recognise the advantages and 
disadvantages of solar energy
● To understand the need to have a suitable 
home design to make the best use of 
solar energy
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware of solar energy 
through observation of panels on roofs, solar 
garden lights and roadside signs. They should 
understand that they experience the energy of the 
sun when they are outdoors, especially in summer. 
Background
Solar power has become a much talked about and 
promoted form of energy. The first major use of solar 
cells was as a backup power supply to the Vanguard 
1 satellite in 1958. Solar power is still used for 
telecommunication satellites and remote stations. 
 
Today, Solar power is used to power offshore 
oil rigs, navigational buoys and railway crossings. It 
is also used for to provide electricity, heating and 
decorative light in domestic homes. 
 
In the past, governments have promoted the 
use of solar energy through rebates and an ability 
to return excess power to the grid. However, it 
takes a number of years to make up the expense of 
installing solar panels. 
 
Like other forms of renewable energy, interest 
and investment in solar energy has been increasing 
globally. Large solar plants are being constructed 
in the United States, Canada, Spain, Mongolia and 
China. 
Starter activity
Lead a class discussion about what solar power is and 
how it is used. Some students might have solar power 
at home – ask them to share their knowledge about 
it. Encourage students to identify advantages and 
disadvantages associated with solar power. Record their 
ideas in a chart or mind map, and put it aside to revisit 
at the end of the unit. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet ‘What is solar power?’, with the 
students. This sheet explores key features of solar power, 
such as where to place solar panels and the need to 
insulate and use energy-efficient appliances. 
 
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Solar 
power’. They will need to refer to the Resource sheet, 
‘What is solar power?’, to complete the questions. This 
activity will reinforce their understanding of the uses 
of solar power both domestically and in larger-scale 
applications. Discuss the use of solar power compared 
with diesel-powered generators or coal-fired power 
stations in terms of emissions of greenhouse gases. 
 
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Advantages and 
disadvantages (1)’, with the class. Encourage the 
students to think of any other advantages or 
disadvantages they could add to the lists. 
 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, 
‘Advantages and disadvantages (2)’. They will need 
to refer to the Resource sheet, ‘Advantages and 
disadvantages (1)’. 
extension activity
Revisit the chart or mind map you made with the 
students for the Starter activity. Work with the class to 
add to the chart, and correct the previous information 
as needed. Ask students to consider the future of 
solar power in Australia, and to give reasons for their 
predictions. Add this information to the chart and 
display it in the classroom.

Teacher’s notes – Indigenous use of the land
Objectives
● To understand what hunting and gathering 
means for a traditional society
● To recognise the sustainable use of the land by 
Indigenous people
● To become familiar with key terms such as: 
Indigenous, inhabitants, remains, archeology, 
tradition, spirituality, prehistoric
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that there were Indigenous 
inhabitants in Australia before British settlement, and 
that there are still Indigenous people today. Some 
Indigenous people live traditional lifestyles today, or 
integrate traditional aspects into their lives. 
Background 
Early Indigenous Australians could only use the 
resources available in their local area. They spent a 
large portion of their daily lives acquiring enough 
food sources. Food also dictated the movement of 
the tribes. 
 
Through their Dreamtime stories, Indigenous 
Australians understood sustainable use of the land, 
and practised this for thousands of years. Tribal 
cultural practices and their food sources differed 
according to their location. There was no cropping, 
although women in some areas replanted some 
roots. Kangaroos and other animals were not tamed 
or used as beasts of burden. Fish traps were built in 
coastal areas like Albany in Western Australian and 
along some inland rivers, but the catch was always 
sustainable.
Starter activity 
Ask students about their understanding of the hunting 
and gathering lifestyle. Discuss how this compares 
with their own lifestyles. You could work with the class 
to research the food sources that were available to 
Indigenous Australians in your local area. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Provide students with the Activity sheet, ‘Indigenous 
Australians and sustainability’. Point out the timescale 
referred to – Mungo Man’s age of about 60 000 years, 
compared to European occupancy of Australia a little 
more than 200 years ago.  Discuss the differences 
between the methods of transferring knowledge and 
cultural practices compared with what happens today. 
Students will need a dictionary or Internet access to 
complete the definitions.
Read the Resource sheet, ‘How did Indigenous 
people live? (1)’ with the students. Discuss the 
sustainability of the Indigenous lifestyle. To extend the 
activity, you could make a class list of the food sources 
of Indigenous Australians, then compile a list of the food 
sources of the students. 
Students will need a copy of the Resource sheet, 
‘How did Indigenous people live? (1)’ to complete 
the Activity sheet, ‘How did Indigenous people live? 
(2)’.  Students will consolidate their understanding of 
the information on the Resource sheet by identifying 
statements that are true or false, and writing their 
own sentences about the lifestyles of the Indigenous 
Australians. 
extension activities
●  Students could use the Internet to research 
Dreamtime stories, particularly those relating to 
finding food, and ensuring food resources were used 
sustainably. 
●  Have the students work in small groups to discuss 
how they could make their own food choices more 
sustainable. Each group could record their ideas as a 
mind map or create a poster.

Teacher’s notes – Sustainable fishing
Background
As the population of the world increases so does the 
demand for fish, especially in developing countries. 
Improved technology has made it easy to locate 
schools of fish, and led to improved fishing methods. 
Some of these methods, such as the use of cyanide, 
the blasting of reefs and bottom trawling cause 
great damage to the environment. Longline and 
purse-seine fishing result in large numbers of fish 
being caught, many as bycatch – fish that are not 
marketable. Many of the bycatch are dead when 
they are thrown back into the ocean. Overfishing 
has resulted in the significant reduction of many fish 
stocks, with some species such as southern bluefin 
tuna becoming critically endangered. Due to market 
demand, much illegal fishing occurs. 
Taking too many fish commercially means there 
is not enough food for marine animals such as 
seabirds, turtles and sharks. Marine parks have been 
established to help protect fish species and to allow 
stocks to replenish, but fisheries say this affects their 
income. Governments have introduced quotas to try 
to make fish stocks sustainable. 
Aquaculture has been used in many places 
around the world for prawns, oysters, mussels, 
barramundi and tuna to supplement the wild 
catch. However, aquaculture farms can cause other 
problems such as contamination from fish food and 
chemicals. 
Starter activity
Discuss the different reasons people have for fishing. 
Bring out the idea that some people fish for fun, some 
for money and other to get the food they need to 
survive. Work with the students to define key fishing 
terms such as wild catch, aquaculture, bycatch and 
overfishing. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Sustainable fishing’, with the 
students. Review the meaning of each term shown in 
bold. Ask students to share any experiences they have 
with fishing and discuss the types of fish they eat. 
 
Provide students with the Resource sheet, ‘Bluefin 
tuna – wild catch or farm?’ Students will need to refer 
to this Resource sheet to complete the questions on 
the Activity sheet, ‘Fishing for bluefin tuna’. Extend the 
activity by leading a discussion about the negative 
impacts of aquaculture, such as the reduction of wild 
stock and the large quantities of anchovies and sardines 
that must be sourced to feed the farmed fish. Ocean 
and coastal pollution also occurs from chemical use and 
dissolved and solid fish waste. 
Have the students read the Resource sheet, ‘Orange 
roughy – overfishing and conservation’. They will 
need to refer to this Resource sheet to complete the 
questions on the Activity sheet, ‘The orange roughy fish’. 
You could extend this activity by having students work 
in small groups to list arguments for and against the 
statement: Fishing for orange roughy should be banned. 
extension activity
●  Students could use the Internet to find more species 
of fish and other marine species that are threatened, 
and possible solutions to these problems. The 
websites of organisations such as the Australian 
Marine Conservation Society, World Wildlife Fund 
and Greenpeace will be useful. 
●  Students could investigate the number of marine 
parks in Australia, map their locations and annotate 
the map to show which marine creatures live there. 
Objectives 
● To learn about the increasing demand for 
fish that results from an increasing human 
population
● To understand the difference between wild 
fishing and aquaculture
● To learn that conservation is essential for the 
sustainability of fishing 
● To appreciate that while fishing is an important 
recreational activity for some people, other 
people rely on the food fishing provides in 
order to survive 
Prior knowledge
Students should know that many people enjoy 
fishing for recreation and that fish is eaten regularly.

Teacher’s notes – Water
Objectives 
● To recognise that water is essential for survival
● To understand how people, plants and animals 
rely on water
● To learn about the need to conserve water 
to ensure sustainability of food supplies and 
communities
Prior knowledge
Students have knowledge of some of the uses of 
water and have some understanding of droughts 
and floods.
Background 
Water is essential for life. All the ecosystems on 
land and within oceans and seas rely on it. Access 
to water is also critical for the production of food 
and industrial products. This is why some rivers 
have been dammed to provide a continual supply. 
Due to people’s need for water, the welfare of the 
environment and habitats for wildlife have at times 
been overlooked.
In recent years, long-term droughts have 
been followed by major floods, such as those in 
Queensland and Victoria in 2011. These floods 
replenish rivers, dams and groundwater as well 
as adding fertile silt to flood plains. However, 
the human cost is enormous through loss of life, 
livelihood, homes and possessions, as well as the 
effect on the Australian economy.
The Murray-Darling Basin is important to the  
3 million people who live in and around the basin 
and depend on the water it provides. The Murray-
Darling Basin is also extremely important to the 
rest of Australia, as one-third of the food supply is 
produced in the region. This contributes $9 billion 
to Australia’s economy through food supply and 
exports such as cotton and rice. 
Starter activity
Brainstorm with the class a list of issues related to 
water; for example, effects of droughts and floods, 
pollution of waterways, global problems such as lack of 
drinking water, local water restrictions, water recycling. 
Guide students to realise that water management is an 
extremely important issue, both now and in terms of 
sustainability for the future.
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Activity sheet, ‘Fact file – water’, with the 
students. Students will unjumble words to complete the 
water facts. Ask the students to identify any facts they 
found surprising, and discuss why. 
Provide the Resource sheet, ‘Case study – Murray-
Darling Basin’. Discuss what the map shows. You could 
have students identify the region on a complete map of 
Australia to assist their understanding of its size. Review 
the key features of maps with the class, and explain the 
meaning of tributary, source and mouth in the context of 
a river system.
Have the students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Using 
the Murray-Darling Basin map’. They will need to refer to 
the Resource sheet, ‘Case study – Murray-Darling Basin’. 
Provide the Resource sheet,  ‘What can be done to 
make the Murray-Darling Basin sustainable?’ and read 
it with the students. Discuss the role of government in 
water management, and the importance of community 
concerns. Introduce the concept of irrigation and give 
examples like Mildura which can exist in an extremely 
dry area and have a thriving agricultural industry 
because of water from the Murray River.
Ask students to complete the Activity sheet, ‘Water 
supply issues’. You could have them use the Internet 
to conduct further research into the issues raised. 
Encourage them to think about these issues and what 
they can do to help make water sustainable. 
extension activity 
●  Collate the water questions students composed on 
the Activity sheet, ‘Water supply issues’. Have them 
work in small groups to answer the questions. 
●  Students could use the Internet to investigate the 
use of water for growing crops like cotton and rice. 
Discuss whether this use of water can be justified. 
Students should identify which crops in Australia 
are sustainable and give reasons. Encourage them 
to consider the issue of cost in terms of equipment, 
infrastructure and time involved in changing 
agricultural products.

Achieve!   Geography – Sustainability in the Asia Pacific
50
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Coral reefs
Objectives 
● To recognise the significance of coral reefs
● To learn about the locations and types of coral 
reefs
● To understand the use and abuse of coral reefs
● To appreciate the need for coral reefs to be 
sustainable
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that the oceans contain 
a huge variety of life, which is important for human 
consumption, recreation and tourism, and essential 
to preserving ecosystems.
Background 
Coral reefs are very complex and fragile ecosystems 
that exist in the oceans. Their ecological significance 
is often compared with that of tropical rainforests 
on the land because of the diversity of species 
found within them. Coral reefs require warm, clear 
water less than 60 metres deep. Their future is 
threatened by fishing, tourism, oil spills, pollution, 
agricultural chemical run-off, silt and sewage. 
Climate change also poses a threat to the 
sustainability of coral reefs.
Starter activity
Ask students to list the kinds of creatures they 
associate with the ocean, and specifically with coral 
reefs. Encourage students to share any experiences 
they have with coral reefs. You could use a mapping 
application such as Google Earth to view coral reefs.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet ‘What are coral reefs?’ introduces 
students to the structure of reefs and the kinds of 
animals that live there. Discuss the meaning of the 
terms in bold. Students could use the Internet to 
help them complete the last activity. To extend the 
activity, you could use the key terms on the sheet to 
start a class pictorial coral reef glossary.
On the Activity sheet, ‘Types of reefs’, students 
complete cloze exercises to explore the three main 
types of reefs, and the underlying structure and 
examples of each type. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Where are coral reefs?’ provides 
an opportunity for students to practise their mapping 
skills. Students will need an atlas or Internet access, 
and a blank world map, the completed Activity sheet, 
‘Types of reefs’, to complete this activity. A map is 
provided on the CD-ROM in the Artwork > Unit 9 
folder. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Life on a coral reef’, provides an 
opportunity for students to investigate the different 
kinds of marine creatures that live around coral reefs. 
Students will need to use the Internet to label marine 
creatures shown in the illustration, then draw and label 
a further list of marine creatures. You could challenge 
students to find the most unusual coral reef creature 
they can to add to the illustration.
On the Activity sheet, ‘Protecting reefs’, students 
explore threats to the reef, and efforts to protect and 
restore reefs. Explain that carbon dioxide from power 
stations and motor vehicles causes warming of the 
atmosphere, which in turn threatens coral reef habitats 
which take thousands of years to form. 
Emphasise sustainability when students complete 
the sentences on the Activity sheet, ‘What can be done 
to ensure that coral reefs are sustainable?’ Discuss the 
idea that all parts of the environment are connected, 
and that people can’t protect an area like a coral reef 
without considering what happens to the water they 
use and the rubbish they generate in their own homes. 
The Resource sheet, ‘How are coral reefs used?’,  
informs students about the ways coral reefs are used 
today, and the increasing number of visitors to coral 
reefs. Encourage them to think of other ways that 
people use coral reefs. 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ‘How can 
people help to save the reefs?’ They may find it useful to 
refer to the Resource sheet, ‘How are coral reefs used?’ 
Encourage them to use the space at the bottom of the 
sheet to list other ways different people can help to 
save coral reefs.
extension activity
Have students work in small groups to create a pictorial 
glossary of marine life around coral reefs. They could 
focus on the creatures in a specific marine park, such as 
the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park or Ningaloo Marine 
Park. To extend the activity, have them identify food 
chains or webs within the marine parks.

Achieve!   Geography – Sustainability in the Asia Pacific
59
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Forests
Objectives
● To understand the importance of forests for the 
production of oxygen
● To appreciate the significance of forests 
providing a sustainable habitat for animals, 
food and medicinal plants
● To learn that demand for timber and other 
products creates problems for the environment
● To learn that the forest products people choose 
to buy can contribute to the conservation and 
sustainability of forests
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that people use forest 
products every day.
Background
Forests in all regions of the earth are extremely 
important as trees take in carbon dioxide and 
produce oxygen. With the climate changing and the 
need to reduce carbon emissions, the conservation 
of forests is crucial to sustainability. The health of 
the planet is not the only factor – we also need 
to manage the ever-growing demand placed on 
forest products by our increasing population. 
This increasing demand has led to the need for 
plantation timber and the preservation of old 
growth timber. Rainforests have been particularly 
vulnerable to wealthy nations using the land for 
oil palms and rubber plantations. Illegal logging 
relies on corruption in countries like Indonesia and 
is aided by the demands for forest products from 
other countries. Environmental organisations like the 
World Wildlife Fund (WWF) are trying to promote 
sustainable forestry in many countries.
Starter activity
Work as a class to make a list of the ways people use 
forests, and the ways people use products made 
from forest resources. Then discuss the sustainability 
of the products made from forest resources, and 
any alternative products people can use that have a 
lower environmental impact.
Resource and Activity sheets
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Forestry (1)’ with the 
students. Discuss the role of forests in sustaining 
biodiversity and providing employment for rangers 
and workers in the timber and tourism industries. 
Ensure students understand the words in bold, 
especially the difference between native and 
plantation forests.
 
Have students complete the Activity sheet, ’Forestry 
(2)’, which provides an opportunity for students to 
review and summarise the information from the 
Resource sheet, ‘Forestry (1)’. Students will need this 
Resource sheet to complete the activity. 
 
On the Activity sheet, ’Protecting East Gippsland’s 
old forests’, students investigate an Australian example 
that highlights the importance of conserving and 
using old-growth forests. The students will use a word 
bank to complete the information.
Provide students with the Resource sheet, 
’Rainforests in Kalimantan, Indonesia’, which shows the 
differences between original rainforest and logged 
rainforest. Encourage students to suggest reasons why 
people log rainforests.
Students could work in pairs or small groups to 
discuss and complete the Activity sheet, ‘Logging 
the forests’. Students will find it useful to refer to the 
Resource sheet, ‘Rainforests in Kalimantan, Indonesia’. 
extension activity
●  As a class, investigate how people can find out 
whether the forest products they use come from 
sustainable sources. 
●  Discuss the environmental problems and social 
issues associated with illegal logging and what can 
be done to prevent it.

Oil, coal and natural gas are fossil fuels.  
They formed over millions of years from

94.8% was supplied by fossil fuels. 
Burning fossil fuels for energy creates  
pollution and releases carbon dioxide into  
the air, which contributes to climate change. 
Fossil fuels are non-renewable resources,

What is wave power?
Every day a huge amount of energy is created by waves pounding the Australian coasts. 
This energy is largely responsible for shaping our coastlines. As renewable energy 
becomes more important, experiments are being conducted to see if electricity can 
be produced economically from this source. Wave power is continuous and does not 
produce greenhouse gas emissions. 
Wave power captures energy from the surface waves, unlike tidal power which uses the 
ebb and flow of the tides. The first wave power farm was built in Portugal in 2006. It can 
produce electricity continuously.
The CETO wave power farm is based in Perth, Western Australia. The diagram below 
shows how it works. 
Resource sheet – Wave power
The CETO wave power converter
These buoys are 
powered by the waves 
to drive pumps that are 
anchored to the sea floor.
The pumps pressurise 
the water, which 
then passes through 
a pipeline to the shore. 
The high-pressure seawater 
then drives turbines, which 
generate electricity without 
producing emissions.
As well as generating electricity, the wave power 
converter can remove the salt from seawater so it can be 
used for drinking or irrigation like any other fresh water.

What is geothermal power?
Geothermal power is a form of renewable energy that comes from heat in the earth’s 
crust. Geo means ‘earth’ and thermal means ‘heat’. For every 100 metres down into the 
earth you go, the temperature increases by about 38C.
Natural geothermal energy
 
●Natural geothermal energy is produced when water seeps into the earth’s crust, 
where it is heated by hot volcanic rocks and then rises to the surface as steam.
 
●In North America, hot springs have been used for cooking for thousands of years. 
 
●In countries such as Indonesia, the Philippines, China, Japan and New Zealand this 
resource has been used for heating, power generation and cooking. 
 
●Five geothermal energy plants are planned for Fergusson Island, which is part of the 
Papua New Guinea archipelago. 
 
●In the Philippines, geothermal power provides 27% of the country’s total electricity 
production. 
Engineered geothermal energy
 
●Australia has a vast amount of hot granite within the earth directly beneath it. This 
could be used to produce power by injecting water into breaks in the rocks, which 
is then returned to the surface as steam. This is called engineered geothermal 
energy because it involves using technology to produce energy from heat deep 
inside the earth. 
 
●South Australia, in particular, has great potential for this form of renewable energy. 
A small geothermal plant capable of generating 520 mega-watts of energy has 
been built at Paralana next to the Beverley Uranium Mine. A plant at the Cooper 
Basin also shows a promising future in hot rock geothermal energy. There are 
thought to be enough hot rocks in South Australia to provide power for all of 
Australia for a very long time. However, the set-up costs for geothermal plants, such 
as the costs of drilling, are high.

now four kilometres thick. This layer insulates the granite, which absorbs heat from deep 
within the earth. The granite four kilometres below the surface has a temperature of more 
than 250°C.

Wind power
Wind is a renewable energy resource – this means that it does not produce carbon 
dioxide or any chemicals that affect public health or the environment. The use of 
renewable energy is an important factor in reducing the impact of climate change and in 
making sure we can continue to produce energy in the future. 
By world standards, Australia has excellent wind resources. The southern coastline lies in the 
roaring forties – between the latitudes of forty and fifty degrees. In this area, strong winds 
blow much of the time, because there is little land in the Southern Hemisphere to stop them.

Opinions about wind farms
Not everyone agrees that wind farms are a good idea. Some people do not like the look 
of wind farms as they are often located in places that are considered areas of beauty, such 
as near the coast or on hills. But are they worse than large power lines?
The wind farm Waubra, 35 km north-west of Ballarat in Victoria, consists of 128 turbines. 
There have been claims of illness caused by the low-level noise of the blades turning. 
Some residents have reported suffering headaches, high blood pressure, rapid heartbeats 
and nausea. One person moved to Ballarat to get away from the noise. His son operates 
the farm but will not live there.
Some people are concerned about the fate of birds and bats that fly into the blades of 
turbines. In northern Tasmania a number of wedge-tailed eagles have been killed as they 
glide on the wind currents (thermals) created by the wind turbines when looking for their prey.
Wind turbines are built-in factories that use a lot of energy, creating pollution. However, 
this occurs only for a short time, unlike the pollution continually created when electricity is 
generated by coal.

What is solar power?
Solar power is renewable energy from the sun which can be converted to electricity. 
Most of Australia has a great deal of sunlight, but there is less in the southern and 
south-eastern areas. To make the most of solar power in homes, it is necessary to have 
energy-efficient heaters, insulation in the walls and ceilings, and solar hot water. Solar 
panels should be placed on north-facing roofs or in open spaces in order to generate the 
most power. 
Case studies
 
●Solar power is extremely effective in small communities like Windorah in 
Queensland, which has a population of 100. Windorah has a group of five solar 
dishes which began generating electricity in 2008. Using them saves 100 000 litres of 
diesel each year, reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 300 tonnes per year.
 
●A Solar Concentrator Power Station is being built near Mildura in Victoria and is 
expected to be fully operational in 2013. The sunlight will be captured by curved 
reflective mirrors which track the sun throughout the day. The project will produce 
enough electricity to power more than 45 000 homes and reduce greenhouse gas 
emissions by about 400 000 tonnes per year.
 
●On average, Mildura receives 2938 hours of sunlight each year. There are 10.7 hours 
of sunlight per day in January and five hours per day in June.
 
●Melbourne receives 2200 hours of sunlight in an average year, with eight hours per 
day in January and four hours per day in June.

Indigenous Australians and 
sustainability
Indigenous Australians are the original inhabitants of Australia and its nearby islands. 
The earliest human remains, dated at about 60 000 years old, are those of Mungo Man.  
He was found in Lake Mungo in New South Wales in 1974.
There is no written record of life in prehistoric Australia. Knowledge about this time 
is found in archeological evidence and in Indigenous oral traditions. Before European 
settlement, all Indigenous Australians based their lifestyles on their Dreaming beliefs. 
The Dreaming (also called the Dreamtime) stories connected humans, animals, fish, birds 
and the land. These connection brought a sense of caring about and spirituality towards 
the land and all the life it supported. The stories explained how to live sustainably so that 
the earth could support all kinds of life, both now and in the future.

35

Achieve!
How did Indigenous people live? (1)
 
●Indigenous Australians were hunter-gatherers who moved according to the 
availability of food. This way, their food supply was sustainable. The types of food 
available depended on whether they lived inland, near rivers or on the coast. The 
men hunted kangaroos, wallabies, echidnas and possums as well as snakes, lizards 
and birds such as ducks, especially along the Murray River. Spears and boomerangs 
made from local trees were used to catch and kill. Fish and eels were caught in traps 
in some areas, such as south-west Victoria.
 
●Fire was used to drive animals out and to ‘clean up’ the land. Fire was also used to 
keep travel corridors open and to encourage the growth of food plants such as 
bracken, daisy yams and grasses so that these resources could be sustained from 
year to year.
 
●Women and young children collected berries, yams, 
seeds, eggs and insects. If they lived near the coast, they 
collected oysters and mussels too. Seeds were ground 
between stones and cooked as cakes.
 
●Indigenous people knew how to hunt and gather 
sustainably so their food supplies would last. For 
example, they did not hunt young kangaroos or take 
more berries than they needed. However, it is thought 
that their practice of using fire did change parts of the 
landscape.
 
●Indigenous people understood the seasons and how 
they affected the food that was available. Along the 
Murray River they caught wildfowl and freshwater 
crayfish in spring, or netted fish in summer. They knew 
how to get groundwater in the desert from springs, rock 
holes and soaks, and dug wells to find water. Water sources  
were regarded as sacred. It was essential for people to  
remember where they were.

Sustainable fishing
The health benefits of eating fish are well known and often promoted. People in many 
countries eat fish every day. Over 1 billion people throughout Asia depend on fish, 
including subsistence islanders in Papua New Guinea and people in the Philippines, who 
depend on fish for their animal protein. Many people are employed making and mending 
boats, nets and other equipment, as well as in fish processing.
In Australia, the fishing industry is number six on the 
list of the most valuable food-based primary industries. 
Almost 3.4 million Australians fish for recreation and 
contribute to the economy by buying fishing licences 
and fishing gear. Some Indigenous Australians fish for 
food, for cultural practices and to earn money. 
As the number of people in the world increases,  
so does the global demand for fish. This, combined  
with changes to methods of fishing, has resulted in 
overfishing. This means that more fish are being  
caught than the ocean can produce, so the  
overall number of fish is decreasing. 
Bycatch is also a significant problem 
– this is the term for the fish and other 
marine creatures that the fisheries catch 
in their nets, but do not want and cannot 
sell. Often these creatures die.
Bluefin tuna is highly valued for its 
flavour, especially when served raw. It 
is overfished in the Pacific Ocean, and 
in most other parts of the world. One 
bluefin tuna caught on a longline off the 
Japanese island of Hokkaido was sold for 
$396,000 in early 2011. That was a price  
of $12,000 per kilo! 
Resource sheet – Sustainable fishing
Purse-seining involves 
putting a long net around a 
group of fish, then closing 
the bottom of the net to 
capture them. 
Midwater trawling involves dragging a 
huge net behind a boat. It catches a large 
number of fish. The use of technology such as 
electronic fish-finders makes it easy to work 
out where the fish are. 
ISBN 978 1 92571 049 6

Achieve!   Geography – Sustainability in the Asia Pacific
40
© Jennifer Leigh-Jones and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Bluefin tuna – wild catch or farm?
Tuna is an extremely popular fish, particularly bluefin tuna, and stocks in the Pacific 
and Indian Oceans are decreasing due to overfishing. With wild catch fishing methods, 
fisheries can catch entire schools of tuna. 
 Southern bluefin tuna are prized as an eating fish, especially for the traditional Japanese 
food sashimi. These tuna live for up to 40 years, grow to two metres long and weighing 
up to 200 kilograms. Due to the high demand for tuna, there are strict quotas in place to 
protect the population. Any fisheries catching more than their quotas are breaking the 
law. Illegal tuna fishing still occurs because people are prepared to pay a great deal of 
money for them.  
Tuna farming at Port Lincoln in South Australia began in the early 1990s. By farming 
the tuna instead of catching them in the wild, the hope is that tuna populations can be 
sustained. However, farming can cause other problems such as contaminating the oceans 
with farm chemicals and the food fed to the fish. Controlling fish diseases is also more 
difficult.
The following information describes how southern bluefin tuna are farmed.
 
●The tuna are caught by purse seine net in the Great Australian Bight in January.
 
●They are transferred live to a towing cage.
 
●The cage is towed very slowly for about 20 days to near Port Lincoln.
 
●The tuna are swum into smaller cages and bred in captivity.
 
●They are fed six days per week, weather permitting.
 
●When there is a growth rate of 40%, usually in  late winter, they are harvested.
 
●They are processed and placed in boxes, frozen or with chill packs.
 
●The fish are then flown to Japan, South-East Asia and Europe. 
Resource sheet – Sustainable fishing
ISBN 978 1 92571 049 6

Conserving the orange roughy
Orange roughy is a bright red fish with a large, bony head and big eyes. It lives in cold, 
deep waters in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans, especially around seamounts 
which are volcanic mountains under the sea. 
This species may live beyond 150 years. It matures between 20 and 40 years of age and 
feeds on prawns, fish and squid. Very young fish are rarely caught by fisheries, but larger 
specimens can be caught well before they can reproduce at about 30 years of age. 
The New Zealand orange roughy fishery is the oldest and largest in the world. It was 
established in the late 1970s and production peaked at approximately 22 000 tonnes in the 
mid-1980s. That figure has now been reduced to about 8650 tonnes. 
In New Zealand, orange roughy fishing is managed under a quota system in a 
200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone, in order to help keep stocks at a sustainable 
level. Measures are being taken to restrict where fish can be caught, and marine national 
parks established to provide a safe place for fish to grow and breed. Similar restrictions 
apply to orange roughy fishing in southern Australian waters.

Where are coral reefs?
You need a world map, an atlas or Internet map search, and the completed Activity sheet, 
‘Types of reefs’.
Coral reefs need special conditions to exist. Coral lives in both temperate and tropical 
waters. Shallow reefs form between the latitudes 308N and 308S. The maximum depth for 
tropical corals to grow is about 60 metres, because the special algae corals contain need 
sunlight. The algae use sunlight and the polyps’ waste products to make oxygen and food 
for the corals to grow. The water must be clean and clear so light can reach the coral. 
The best seawater temperatures for growth are 24–31°C. This is why there are no reefs 
near the mouths of major rivers like the River Ganges and the Indus River, which carry very 
dirty water. Coral reefs don’t grow in places where rivers meet the ocean. This is because 
the rivers put nutrients, pollution and fresh, colder water into the ocean.

Forestry (1)
Resource sheet – Forests
Forests are extremely important to the health of the earth. They absorb carbon, 
which is emitted when fossil fuels are burned. Forests produce oxygen, which 
people and animals need to live. They also provide wood, which people use to 
construct houses and other buildings, and to manufacture products such as furniture 
and paper. 
Forests provide a habitat for animals, birds and a great variety  
of plants that provide fruit and medicines.
About 19% of Australia is covered with forest. Native forests cover approximately 
147 million hectares, and plantation forests cover approximately 2 million hectares. 
Plantation forests contain trees such as pines and blue gums, for commercial use.
Forests must have water, soil and nutrients to survive.  
Many forest catchments provide an important source of  
drinking water for towns and cities.
Some people in Tasmania and Victoria do not want old-growth forests logged 
because biodiversity is lost, as are the habitats of birds, animals and plants.
Many old-growth forests are in national parks and state parks. Picnic areas, camping 
grounds, bushwalking tracks and nature walks are available in many parks.

Fighting for  
the Empire
During World War 1, Australians saw 
England as the ‘mother country’. Many 
Australians wanted to fight with the British 
Empire because of this special relationship. 
+ 1	 Read Effie Kiel’s essay. Underline 
the words that show the writer 
feels she is a part of the British 
Empire. One example has been 
underlined already. 
2	 Describe how this source supports the 
point of view that many Australians felt 
they had a special relationship with the 
British Empire.
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
THE BRITISH EMPIRE.
A CHILD’S ESSAY.
At the Buln Buln East State school in connection 
with the celebration of Empire Day, a prize was 
given for the best essay on “The British Empire” 
and the prize was awarded to Miss Eff ie Kiel, 
whose essay was as follows:—
THE BRITISH EMPIRE.
The British Empire is the largest and greatest 
Empire in the World. An Empire can be great 
without being large, but the British Empire is both 
great and large. Our King rules over 400,000,000 
subjects or 24% of the earth’s population. If we 
look at the map of the world we will see that 
many places are colored red, this means that 
these places belong to the British Empire. If 
they were put together they would form a tract of 
land 12,000,000 square miles in area.
	 We can all help to make the Empire great. One man 
could not make an Empire; statesmen, explorers, 
scientists, soldiers, sailors, and many others 
are needed to make one. The British Empire was 
not formed in one year, neither was it formed 
in one hundred years. Men have been building 
it up for hundreds of years, men such as Drake, 
Raleigh, Hawkins, Blake, Nelson, Clive, Pitt, 
Wolfe and Cook. 
	 What is the reason of our Empire being so 
great? There are many reasons. Great Britain 
is surrounded by water, and thus while the 
neighboring countries were f ighting she had time 
to colonize other places. The British people are 
fond of the sea and so they are able to effectively 
protect her colonies. We should be careful not 
to become lazy or proud as our Empire will then 
decay as the Roman and Spanish Empires did. 
	 The British people have always been fond of 
liberty, but sometimes they have denied this to 
others. They taxed the Americans unjustly and 
the opium trade is a blot on their fame; but they 
treat their colonies fairly. We have one flag the 
Union Jack (red, white and blue,) the colors of 
the Empire stand for courage, purity and loyalty. 
The Union Jack floats in almost every part of the 
world and wherever we see it, it reminds us of 
the great British Empire and our responsibility 
as citizens of it. EFFIE KIEL, 12 yrs, 9 mos.

‘The Big Picture’ 
Tom Roberts’s artwork documented the opening of the first parliament of Australia in Melbourne, 
May 1903. His artwork was called ‘The Big Picture’ and it was created before World War 1 started in 
1914. It includes 269 portraits of people who attended the event. Think about what this artwork 
shows about the relationship between Australia and the British Empire.

•  three judges wearing wigs at the front
•  the Duke of Cornwall (later King George V) on the stage 
making a speech
•  the Prime Minister of Australia, Edmund Barton, standing 
in front of the stage, with papers, facing the Duke
•  two female members of the Royal family in long dresses 
behind the Duke
•  a large crown behind the stage
•  a row of large flags in the centre of the print
•  the large shaft of sunlight in the top right of the print
•  two men in religious robes (skull cap, tall black hat) in 
the bottom left corner

Nursing at The Front
Matron Mary Anne (Bessie) Pocock (1863-1946) was an Australian nurse who served in the Boar 
War and World War 1. She received medals for her service and was described as a kind and highly 
organised nurse. These quotes are from her diary, written in 1916 when Pocock served in France. 
Resource sheet – The nature of warfare
July 6th 
Nothing in the tent to work with DREADFUL! Sister came to help 
about 9/30am. Such bad cases, poor boys, so dirty and tired. Some 
had laid out for several days, they told me. Jaw cases very bad, 
chest also. 5 operations – excise eyes, 20 operations on eyes today 
and 5 of those, both eyes gone. Poor chaps. Terrible – Terrible!
Got straight this afternoon. M.O.’s coming in all day – seeing 
eyes. Seem to forget that you are alone, trying to do all the 
smashed up and wash some dirt of(f) your men. 
. . . No time off for anyone hardly today.
July 17th
If rations are good enough for men working in trenches etc. it 
is good enough for these women . . . Aeroplane over our tents this 
morning – so close to us. 
July 22nd
Very cold again. Did not sleep so well today . . . We do not get 
enough to eat – 2 sardines and one boiled egg alternatively. 
Awfully bad food and not enough of it. 
July 24th
Some buttercups blooming at my bedside in the tent. Grass a 
foot high about 6 feet by 4. Every other place I’ve had a tent 
the floor has been covered with boards, both for patients and 
sisters, nothing is done here like any other place though. 
August 3rd
Guns very noisy and frequent – hardly ever stop. Not many 
patients considering all the gun f ire. Some more men during the 
night – still today, abdominal wounds – leg – head cases – another 
appendicitis. 
1 Maori, leg amputated this morning. 
Source: AWM PR05050 – Papers of Sister Mary Anne “Bessie” Pocock 
ISBN 978-0-6481150-7-6

Chemical warfare
Chemical warfare was used by both the German army and Allied armies during World War 1. 
Thousands of soldiers were killed and injured by chemical weapons. 
+ Use these primary sources to write a personal diary entry in your workbook from the point 
of view of an Australian soldier affected by mustard gas. Describe where you are and the 
effects of the gas on you and other soldiers. 
Activity sheet – The nature of warfare
Source 1
Gassed Australian soldiers lying out in the 
open at an over crowded aid post near Bois 
l’Abbé, 27 May 1918. Note on the source 
by Sergeant A. Brooksbank, Gas NCO, 10th 
Australian Infantry Brigade: “Examples of 
what should not be done. Casualties should 
have removed contaminated garments. 
Lying on the ground with contaminated 
clothes and not wearing respirators means 
that they are inhaling quantities of vapour 
and adding to their injuries”. AWM E04851
Source: Excerpt from the diary (16 October

Oct 2nd
. . . We had a bad time from moustard gas 
today & a number of us are affected in the 
throat & eyes. My throat is particularly 
bad at present. It has made many of us feel 
sick lately & some are sick. It is always 
lying about in the low country. We have to be 
careful not to walk near the places where the 
gas shells fall as it would eat your boots off 
your feet. You must not let it come in contact 
with the flesh. Same effect as the boots.

Private William Allan Irwin
More than 1250 Indigenous Australian men served in World War 1. 
Over 50 fought in the Gallipoli campaign. Hundreds of Indigenous 
men were killed or wounded and more than thirty Indigenous 
men received medals for bravery. 
Private William Allan Irwin 
Born at the Burra Bee Dee Aboriginal Mission Station near 
Coonabarabran, New South Wales, the 37-year-old shearer 
enlisted in January 1916. He fought with the 33rd Australian 
Infantry Battalion. In 1918, after his death, Irwin was awarded the 
Distinguished Conduct Medal (DCM). His citation reads:

Irregularly enlisted 
Resource sheet – Indigenous Australians at war
EMPTY SADDLES FILLED.
UNIQUE SCENE AT RECRUITING RALLY.
	 There was a unique scene during the progress 
of the Empire Day recruiting rally at the Post 
Off ice yesterday. Until a week or two ago the 
Federal authorities had set their face against 
the enlistment of half-caste aboriginals, but now 
this condition has been waived. Following on this 
decision Chaplain Lieut.-Colonel Garland visited 
the aboriginal settlement at Barambah, where a 
number of half-castes promptly answered the call of 
the Empire. Yesterday a batch of 17 attended at the 
recruiting rally, without uniform. Shortly after 
1 o’clock the members of this newest acquisition 
to the Australian Imperial Force marched down 
Queen-street and drew up at the Post Off ice steps. 
Here Chaplain Lieut Colonel Garland delivered 
a stirring address to the thousands who had 
assembled, and during his address a long line of 
Light Horsemen, each soldier leading a horse with 
an empty saddle, trotted down Queen-street past 
the recruiting base. Chaplain Garland referred to 
his visit to Barambah, and expressed the opinion 
that very soon there would not be half a dozen 
eligible half-caste aboriginals left at Barambah. 
(Applause.) He felt sure that they would be welcomed 
as brothers and quickly made the pets of the unit 
to which they were attached. A lot was said about 
a white Australia, yet here we had the spectacle 
of half-caste aboriginals going to reinforce our 
soldiers simply because those “things” who held up 
veranda posts would not do their duty. He believed 
that Australia was worth f ighting for, but he was 
beginning to believe that there were people in 
Australia who were not worth f ighting for. It made 
his heart bleed to see the married men, the men 
over 45 years of age, the men growing old and the 
men with three, f ive, and seven children having to 
come forward simply because the young, un-married 
men would not do their duty.
	 Amid a scene of great enthusiasm, Chaplain 
Lieutenant-Colonel Garland gave the oath to a half-
caste from Barambah, bringing the total recruits 
secured from that centre to 17. The Light Horsemen 
then rode up, and amid considerable cheering the 
new recruits each mounted a riderless horse and 
proceeded up Queen-street, riding with the ease so 
characteristic of the Australian aboriginal.
ABORIGINAL RECRUITS.
	 We have received from Barambah 
Settlement a letter written on behalf of 
16 discharged coloured soldiers who want 
to know why they were discharged from the 
A.I.F. on June 13. They resent being made 
to appear as “slackers,” through no fault 
of their own. And they allege that when 
they were discharged from the military 
camp they were told that they would be 
met at the Central Railway Station by the 
Chief Protector of Aborigines, who would 
hand over to them their pay and discharge 
papers. Instead they were at the station 
handed over to a police escort, and were 
brought back to their settlement “like a 
lot of prisoners.“ The letter concludes: 
“We will ask the public of Brisbane 
and Murgon if us coloured members of 
the Empire who risked our lives and 
volunteered for the freedom and liberty 
of the British Empire got a fair do or not. 
Also we never got our pay or discharge 
papers.”
	 The military authorities explain that 
headquarters at Melbourne only gave 
approval for coloured men to be enlisted 
on condition that one of the parents was 
of European origin. That condition was 
later on qualif ied to the effect that a 
coloured man must have been associated 
with white people for some time prior to 
enlistment. The men rejected were stated 
by the military authorities to be full- 
blooded aboriginals. When they arrived at 
the camp they were specially examined by 
a medical off icer, and were subsequently 
removed from the camp as unf it for 
military duties. They were not half-
castes, and the military authorities state 
that full-blooded aboriginals are not 
wanted, as they will not make soldiers. 
The instructions issued to headquarters 
at Brisbane state that half-castes can 
be enlisted at the discretion of the 
commandant. It was pointed out that white 
men have an objection to a “blackfellow” 
being associated with them at the camp.
Source 1: The Brisbane Courier, p7 Friday 25 May 1917 
https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/20142091
Source 2: The Brisbane Courier, p 7 Wednesday June 20 
1917. https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/20172809

Harry Blake 
Indigenous men could only enlist if they were believed to 
have some white European heritage and had spent time 
with white people. Recruit Harry Blake is one of the men in 
Source 2, ‘Aboriginal recruits’, who enlisted and was then later 
discharged because he was said to be ‘irregularly enlisted’. 
+ Use the primary sources on the Resource sheet, 
‘Irregularly enlisted’, to answer the questions.
Source 1 – ‘Empty saddles filled’

tell you about attitudes towards Indigenous people at this time in Australian history? 
	
	
2	 Write one fact reported in this newspaper column. How do you know it is a fact and not an 
opinion? 
	
	
	
	
3	 Summarise one opinion expressed by the writer of the newspaper column.
	
	
	
	
Source 2 – ‘Aboriginal Recruits’
4	 What did the Indigenous men want?

Assessing the reliability of sources

The boxing soldier
Source 1: Alfred ‘Tiny’ Ryan

Enlistment date: 29 January 1915
Source 2
Resource sheet – Indigenous Australians at war
The Sun, Sydney, page 14, Sunday 15 August, 1915  
Excerpts from the newspaper column written by W.F. Cordett. 
The well-known N.S.W. western district heavyweight Tiny Ryan 
is lying wounded at Heliopolis, Cairo. His letter to me, dated 
June 26, supplies the following address, which I give in the 
hope that some of his friends may write to him: No. 1802, 2nd 
Battalion, 4th Reinforcements, A.I.E.F., 1st Brigade, Egypt-  
He says:
Since my last letter to you from on board the transport I have 
had pneumonia, got better, went over to the Dardanelles, and 
have been wounded, and I am once more back in Cairo, and am 
getting along famously since an operation upon my head.
. . . These bombs make a very powerful explosion. We have Indian 
mountain batteries with us, and the Indians give the Turks 
some hurry up when they send a 12-pounder in among them. 
Things are fairly quiet in the Australian trenches at the time 
of writing, but at Achi Baba, where the Tommies and French are, 
there is always something doing.
... I saw the Triumph sink just below our trenches. It was 
torpedoed by a submarine. The Queen Elizabeth is a big ship, and 
when she lets go you can bet your life there is something doing.
Aboriginal Natives of Australia, The 
Bogan River Tribe 1898, The child 
Alfred Ryan is seated on the log. 
© Bert Morris. Bert’s grandfather 
took the original image.

Good enough to fight, but not good enough 
to vote
During World War 1, Indigenous Australians were unable to vote. Laws controlled where they lived 
and worked and who they married. Indigenous Australians fought for their country, but as a group 
they did not gain full voting rights until the 1960s and were not counted in the Census until 1967. 
+ Use the three sources on the Resource sheet, ‘The boxing soldier’, to complete the activity.
	
	
Imagine you are Private Alfred Ryan. Read the three sources again. Then write a letter 
reflecting on your life, from growing up in rural New South Wales in 1898 to lying in the 
hospital in Cairo in 1915.

THE DINKUMS’ REFERENDUM CAMPAIGN.
“Our only concern is that the 
mates we have left behind in the 
trenches shall be given the help 
they need. We know only too well 
how badly they require that help. 
Will you allow your thousands of 
unmarried, unencumbered men to 
continue to live at ease under the 
sheltering wings of the British 
fleet and listen to your sons 
and brothers on the battlef ield 
appealing to you night and day for 
help? Will you allow these things 
to go on and refuse to stretch out 
the helping hand? Not if you are 
true Australians!” 
F. P. J. KILLEEN.
‘The Dinkums’ Referendum Campaign’ F.P.J Killeen. 
Sydney Mail (NSW: 1912-1938), Wednesday 
12 December 1917, page 38
https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/
article/160629509

The argument for ‘Yes’

Poster, David Low  
c. 1916-17  
AWM ARTV10140 
Source 1
‘Voice from the trenches’ Sydney Mail (NSW: 1912-1938), 
Wednesday 12 December 1917, page 38
Source 3
CAPTAIN ARTHUR SEAFORTH BLACKBURN, who 
won the Victoria Cross for an action in 
which, at the head of 50 men, be directed 
a drive against an enemy strong point 
with dogged determination, and eventually 
captured a trench, writes: — ‘From the 
bottom of my heart I pray the electors of 
Australia to register an aff irmative vote on 
December 20 next. No person with any sense 
of justice or truth can deny that voluntary 
recruiting has failed to keep up a proper 
supply of reinforcements for our boys at the 
front. I know how desperately those boys 
are in need of help. I know that the fate of 
those boys — aye, their very lives — depends 
upon whether Australia will send them help, 
and so I say to the people of Australia that, 
voluntaryism having failed to keep up the 
supply of reinforcements, every ‘No’ vote cast 
on December 20 is a deliberate, cold-blooded 
desertion of the men in the trenches: nay, 
more, it is a deliberate condemnation to 
death of the men in the trenches.

Welcome home 
Sapper Arthur Findon Dunbar was 30 years old when he enlisted in late 1915.  
He returned home to South Australia on 26 June 1919. 
Sapper Dunbar  
was awarded the  
Military Medal:

Company, July -

Sapper Dunbar removed several dangerous booby traps from dugouts 
and assisted in the capture of many prisoners. He also detected 
and removed a large number of road mines. The whole of the day he 
worked under heavy shell and machine gun f ire, during which 50% 
of his party became casualities.
Source: Australian War Memorial Honours and awards list. Compiled from London and

The Digger’s idol
Prime Minister Billy Hughes returned to Australia in September 1919 after being very involved in 
the outcomes of the Paris Peace Conference. Many returned soldiers celebrated his achievements 
at the conference, even though Hughes supported conscription during World War 1. 
Resource sheet – The economy and society
Definitions
Diggers: Australian 
soldiers
fitness: suitability
cavil: make 
unnecessary or 
unimportant objections
peculiarly: noticeably, 
clearly
Source: The Mirror (Sydney, NSW : 1917 - 1919) Sun 14 Sep 1919, Page 1
Mr Hughes has been hailed as the Digger’s 
Friend. Some people may cavil at the title, but 
the diggers themselves plainly have no doubts 
about the f itness of it. They regard the Prime 
Minister as peculiarly their own man. They have

Prime Minister John Howard (1996–2007) believed that the battle at Gallipoli was the place

And also today we think of those still abroad in our name in places such

But as importantly, we gather in ever-increasing numbers to each 
pledge anew our determination, not merely to dwell upon the legacy 
of the past, but also to build upon it. To extend a culture of proud 
self reliance and personal initiative. To create a just society where 
an individual’s rights are respected but their responsibilities are also

of the world should they only have the heart and the will to grasp them.

Achieve!   History – Japan under the shoguns 1
5
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Introducing shogunate Japan
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge is required for this unit.
Background
Japan, although a small country, has a rich and 
multifaceted history, particularly during the medieval 
or shogunate period. Although it lasted much 
longer, this period in Japan is strikingly similar to the 
European medieval age in terms of how their societies 
were structured. Both places had a strongly feudal 
structure to their societies. There was also a warrior 
class – in medieval Europe there were the knights, 
while in medieval Japan there were the samurai. 
Starter activity
In groups, ask students to brainstorm what they know 
about medieval Japan. Encourage them to share 
their ideas as a class, and ask them where they got 
their information from. Sources may include movies, 
television, the internet, books, etc. Discuss how 
valuable, complex or unreliable these sources could 
be. For example, movies can be unreliable sources 
because the writers are trying to tell a story, so don’t 
always focus on the facts. Textbooks can be valuable 
sources because the information they contain had to 
be checked before printing.
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Key terms’, should be read 
through before completing the Activity sheet, 
‘Imperial Japan’. The words and definitions will be 
very important for students to understand as they 
work through the unit. You may also wish to refer 
to page 25, ‘Japanese hierachy’, in Unit 4, for further 
information.
The Activity sheet, ‘Japanese lands’, introduces students 
to Japan as a nation made up of many islands, and the 
implications this had for the way it was ruled. Students 
colour in a map to consolidate their understanding. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Japan and its neighbours’, presents 
a cloze activity describing Japan’s relationships with its 
nearest neighbours. 
The last Activity sheet, ‘How the emperors lost power’, 
provides students with some background to the rise of 
the shoguns.
Extension ideas
•	 Students could research myths and legends about 
the creation of Japan.
•	 Students could compare the kinds of transport used 
in ancient Japan to the forms of transport used 
today, either in Japan or in Australia, focusing on the 
reasons those forms are used.
Objectives
•	 Identify important historical features of and 
terms relating to shogunate Japan
•	 Identify recognised historical periods for 
shogunate Japan
•	 Understand how the shape of the land led to 
the use of certain forms of transport
•	 Develop an understanding of the relationships 
between Japan and its neighbouring countries

Achieve!   History – Japan under the shoguns 1
11
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Beginning of the shogunate
Prior knowledge
Students should be familiar with the key terms 
introduced on the ‘Key terms’ Resource sheet in Unit 1 
(see page 6).
Background
It is important to remember that with Japanese names, 
the surname is generally written first. For example, 
Minamoto Yoritomo was the head of the Minamoto 
clan. Minamoto was his family name and Yoritomo 
was his given name. 
Clans or families were very important in shogunate 
Japan. Members of large extended families often 
had to follow the head of their clan or they would be 
punished. Some people were assassinated, or forced 
into the priesthood (cloistered) if they did not obey 
the leader of their family. 
People living in shogunate Japan often changed their 
names. Sometimes both the first and last name were 
changed to signify different events, and both partners 
would sometimes change their names when they got 
married. The names used in textbooks are usually the 
names that the person was most commonly known 
by, as some people may have had five or six different 
names. Minamoto Yoritomo’s wife is often referred to 
as Hojo Masaka; this is her original family name. This is 
probably because she was mentioned more and had 
more power as a member of her family clan than of 
her husband’s clan.
Many women did not have their names recorded. 
Sometimes the name given for a woman in history 
textbooks is not actually her first or last name but, 
rather, the name of the place she lived in. 
Starter activity
Ask students to think about their families. Why are 
families so important? What do we expect them to do 
for us? What do we do for them? Explain that although 
nowadays many people have closer relationships with 
their friends, in the past, families were particularly 
important. The family was often involved in choosing 
who you would marry, as well as involving you in any 
fights they had. 
In small groups, have students discuss the differences 
between the role of the family now compared to 
in ancient Japan. Encourage them to consider the 
following question: Would they go to war with 
another family if their family told them they had to?
Resource and Activity sheets
In the Activity sheet, ‘Fujiwara clan’, students read 
about the Fujiwara clan and then answer questions 
exploring the clan’s actions. In the Activity sheet, ‘The 
battle to rule Japan’, students complete a cloze activity 
describing the power struggle between the different 
clans. The Activity sheet, ‘Minamoto clan’, introduces 
the rule of the Minamoto and then the Hojo clans. This 
sheet is best worked through as a class. Encourage 
students to identify key words, and help them define 
any unclear terms. Key words often identify the 
people, places, dates and important actions described 
in a document.
In the Activity sheet, ‘Mongol invasion’, students 
identify common and proper nouns in a passage. It 
may help to take students through the differences 
between common and proper nouns before this task is 
attempted. The Activity sheet, ‘Age of warring states’, 
encourages students to consider different perspectives 
on this period, demonstrating how people can be both 
advantaged and disadvantaged by war.
Extension ideas
•	 Students could research one of the following clans 
in more detail: Fujiwara, Ashikaga, Minamoto, Hojo 
or Taira. Ask them to find out five important facts 
about their chosen clan.
•	 Have students read the ‘The battle to rule Japan’ 
Activity sheet and then ask them to write a diary 
entry or report from the Taira perspective and one 
from the Minamoto perspective. How did the clans 
see the events differently?
•	 Ask students to list five things they have learned 
from the unit, three things they could teach and one 
question they still don’t know the answer to. They 
could also research the answer to their question.
•	 Students could identify the differences between 
war in the past and war in modern times, listing at 
least five differences, such as locations, weapons, 
people who became soldiers, and transport.
Objectives
•	 To gain a basic understanding of the sequence 
of events in Japanese history
•	 To learn about the external threats to Japan
•	 To identify the reasons for change and conflict 
in the power relations in Japan

17
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Tokugawan shogunate
Prior knowledge
Students should have a basic understanding of the 
timeline of shogunate Japan, and be familiar with key 
terms such as daimyo, shogun and emperor. 
Background
The Tokugawan shogunate was one of the longest-
lasting shogun families. Their long reign was due to 
the strength of their leader and founder, Tokugawa 
Ieyasu. He was a strong leader who was very 
controlling of his followers and subjects, determined 
that there would never again be a time of warring 
states. The lack of control he had over his own life 
when he was young made him even more determined 
to control the lives of those around him.
Starter activity
What is a good leader? What qualities do they need to 
have? Ask the class to brainstorm ideas about leaders. 
Then have them suggest examples of good leaders – 
people who are able to motivate and inspire others. 
Remind the students that this could include those who 
were not necessarily seen as good people, but who 
may have been good leaders. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘End of warring states’, explains 
how Oda Nobunaga managed to briefly gain control 
of all of Japan, before being killed. Students may 
need some terms clarified before completing the 
tasks. The last question could be used to prompt a 
class discussion – students should suggest realistic 
possibilities, such as the child gaining power, the child 
being killed, etc. The reality was that Tokugawa Ieyasu 
took control, although he let the child live.  
The Activity sheet, ‘Tokugawa Ieyasu’s childhood’, 
presents a cloze activity outlining the life and times 
in which Ieyasu grew up. Students may wish to use a 
dictionary to help them with any unfamiliar terms in 
the word banks.
Students should read the Resource sheet, ‘The rise of 
Tokugawa Ieyasu’, before they complete the Activity 
sheet, ‘Tokugawa Ieyasu’. The Resource sheet provides 
students with an understanding of Tokugawa Ieyasu 
and how he took power.
Students learn about primary and secondary sources 
in the Activity sheet, ‘Tokugawan shogunate’. They are 
asked to consider the advantages and disadvantages 
of secondary sources and learn how to identify 
primary sources. 
Extension ideas
•	 Students could complete a short research task on 
Tokugawa Ieyasu, Oda Nobunaga or Toyotomi 
Hideyoshi and create a small pamphlet or poster to 
present the information.
•	 In four small groups, students could create a 
role-play based on Tokugawa Ieyasu being taken 
hostage (see the ‘Tokugawa Ieyasu’s childhood’ 
Activity sheet). Students could write some dialogue 
and perform their role-play for the class. 
–– Group A could focus on how Tokugawa Ieyasu 
would have felt. Would he have expected to be 
rescued? 
–– Group B could focus on explaining Tokugawa 
Ieyasu’s father’s reaction. Why might he have said 
that Oda Nobuhide could kill his son?
–– Group C could focus on explaining why Oda 
Nobuhide didn’t end up killing Tokugawa Ieyasu. 
This was a violent time; why didn’t he kill the 
child?
–– Group D could focus on how Tokugawa Ieyasu’s 
mother would have reacted. She was married to 
someone connected to the Oda clan. How would 
she have felt knowing that her son could have 
been killed by her new family?
Objectives
•	 To learn about the conflicts behind the quest 
for power
•	 To understand the origins of the founder of the 
longest-lasting shogunate

Achieve!   History – Japan under the shoguns 1
23
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Occupations
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge is required for this unit.
Background
Japanese feudal society was strictly divided into 
distinct classes or groups. It was rare, although not 
impossible, for people to move from one group to 
another. One of the shoguns, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, was 
born the son of a peasant. Some merchants managed 
to become daimyo by paying large sums of money 
or marrying into a wealthy family. The daimyo had 
complete power over the people in their lands, and 
could make them join armies, follow particular laws or 
pay very high taxes. The samurai and the peasants had 
to remain loyal to their daimyo.
Starter activity
You may wish to show students a diagram of medieval 
European feudal society, as the structure was quite 
similar to shogunate Japan. Students may be more 
familiar with terms such as kings, lords and knights, 
so comparing the structures may help students to 
understand the Japanese shogunate world. Ask 
students to create their own diagrams of the structure 
of shogunate Japanese society. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Feudal Japan’, introduces 
the structure of feudal society and the roles and 
responsibilities of the different groups. Regarding 
the last question on the Activity sheet, many of 
the occupations listed did not fit into the feudal 
structure because they did not rely on the giving of 
land for service. Those occupations relied on money, 
rather than land and mutual obligations. ‘Unclean’ 
occupations dealt with death or bloodshed, which the 
Japanese considered polluting.
The Resource sheet, ‘Japanese hierarchy’, explains in 
more detail the different classes in Japanese society, 
identifying the highest and lowest members. Students 
can use this information to complete the Activity 
sheet, ‘Different jobs’. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Lowest classes’, illustrates the 
differences in the lifestyles of the lower-class citizens 
and the daimyo. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Women’, examines the role of 
women in Japanese society. In a patriarchal society, 
women’s contributions were often disregarded or 
seen as less important. The Activity sheet encourages 
students to compare and contrast this with the roles of 
women in modern society.
Extension ideas
•	 Students could research a famous woman in feudal 
Japan, such as Mugai Nodai, Tomoe Gozen, Lady 
Murasake Shikibu or Sei Shonagan.
•	 Have students find a diagram of European 
feudal society and list three similarities and three 
differences between it and feudal Japanese society.
•	 Students could imagine that they are from a 
particular class in feudal Japan and write a diary 
entry describing a typical day in their life.
•	 Students could create a mind map of occupations  
in feudal Japan.
Objectives
•	 To learn about the structure of shogunate 
Japanese society
•	 To understand the roles and relationships in 
Japanese society
•	 To explore gender roles in a patriarchal society

Achieve!   History – Japan under the shoguns 1
29
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Lifestyles
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge is required for this unit.
Background
Cultural activities have always played a large role in 
Japanese society. Although war and soldiers were 
highly important during the shogunate period, the 
Japanese defined themselves more through their 
cultural activities than through their warlike practices. 
They considered those who did not engage in cultural 
activities to be barbaric. Many Japanese cultural 
activities originally began as religious activities  
that were connected to one of the two main religions, 
Buddhism or Shintoism. Over time these became  
part of everyday life.
Starter activity
Ask students what a cultural activity is. Once they have 
defined this successfully, ask them to suggest different 
cultural activities that they have participated in or 
viewed. Have students identify why these activities are 
seen as important cultural activities. You may also wish 
to follow up with a discussion about the idea of each 
student’s own cultural identity. What is your cultural 
identity? How is it shaped by the cultural activities we 
participate in? 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Religion’, introduces the main 
religions followed in shogunate Japan. Students 
identify the differences between the core beliefs of 
each religion. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Culture’, introduces some of 
the cultural activities enjoyed in shogunate Japan. 
Students identify words to complete a passage 
describing each practice. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘Poetry’, students use the 
information about Japanese poetry to write their 
own poem. They may need additional information on 
syllables in order to understand how to create a haiku.
Before students complete the Activity sheet, ‘Female 
authors’, you may wish to have a class discussion 
about the importance of reading about female 
experiences in history, as so much recorded history 
was written by men. Students will read short primary 
sources from the authors and use these to identify 
information about the time period.
The Activity sheet, ‘Education’, provides students with 
an overview of the types of education in shogunate 
Japan, and invites them to compare this to their own 
lives.
Extension ideas
•	 Students may choose to research and read poetry 
by Matsuo Basho. Ask them to choose their favourite 
poems and explain why these poems appealed to 
them.
•	 Students could discuss the difference between 
religion in shogunate Japan and the way religion 
is seen today. Can you follow two religions today? 
Why was religion so important then? Have people’s 
views about religion changed?
•	 Students could create a chart comparing the cultural 
activities in shogunate Japan with those enjoyed in 
modern-day society.
•	 Students could create a short dramatic performance 
in the Noh or Kabuki styles of theatre. This might 
include making masks for their characters.
•	 Ask students to imagine that they are Sei Shonagan 
or Murasaki Shikibu (two famous female authors). 
Have them write a diary entry describing their 
experiences in court. 
Objectives
•	 To learn about important elements of 
shogunate Japanese society
•	 To develop an understanding of different 
cultural activities and practices

Achieve!   History – Japan under the shoguns 1
35
© Rachel Towns and Blake Education 2014
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Samurai
Prior knowledge
Students should be familiar with key terms such as 
daimyo and shogun.
Background
The Japanese samurai were very much like the knights 
of Europe. They were highly trained, familiar with 
weapons and followed a code of conduct. The code 
of conduct followed by European knights was called 
chivalry. Many of the knights followed Christianity  
and became involved in crusades to protect their 
religion. The Japanese samurai likewise followed 
a code of conduct, called Bushido. Both codes 
emphasised defending the weak and showing  
loyalty to a lord. Many of the Japanese samurai were 
also Zen Buddhists who used meditation and other 
aspects of their religion to help them keep their focus 
when fighting. 
Starter activity
Ask students what they already know about samurai. 
Can they name any other types of Japanese warriors? 
They may discuss ninjas or even the ronin. If the 
students are more familiar with European history, it 
may be interesting to do a comparison between the 
European knights and Japanese samurai. Draw up a 
table on the board listing the name, code of conduct 
and religion of each group. 
Resource and Activity sheets
Students can read the Resource sheet, ‘Samurai’, 
before using the information from it to complete the 
Activity sheet, ‘Warrior lives’.
Students can then read through the Resource sheet, 
‘Bushido’, then imagine themselves in the role of a 
samurai to complete the Activity sheet, ‘Way of the 
warrior’. This task is best completed in pairs. Students 
should understand that there are no right or wrong 
answers – the activity reflects their views. They should 
be able to back up their opinions, however.
The Activity sheet, ‘Crime and punishment’, presents a 
cloze activity outlining the code of honour, crime and 
punishment followed by the samurai. Students must 
read the paragraphs carefully in order to fill in the 
blanks correctly. This activity helps students to read 
sentences in context using grammatical skills.
Extension ideas
•	 Have students create a glossary of the following 
terms: samurai, bushido, ronin, ninja, bushi, daimyo.
•	 Students could attempt to complete tasks 
blindfolded in order to understand the difficulty of 
samurai training. These could be simple tasks, such 
as writing a letter or following a trail through a room. 
Consideration should be given to student safety. 
•	 Students could write a diary entry describing a day 
in the life of a samurai.
•	 Students could create a recruitment poster 
advertising the key requirements of a samurai.  
Hint: this should refer to fighting skills, cultural 
activities and Bushido.
Objectives
•	 To learn about the warrior culture of shogunate 
Japan
•	 To develop an understanding of Bushido, or 
the warriors’ code
•	 To understand the role that samurai played in 
Japanese society
•	 To develop an understanding of crime and 
punishment in Japanese society
